subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-139 before the House today contains more than 500 pages of legislation, does not even have an index and is a collection of extremely complex clauses. Curious though that may seem, Mr. Speaker, while the White Paper was tabled in June 1987 and amended in December 1987, this is the first opportunity the House has had to debate this reform in this Chamber.
Granted, the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs has considered the question for a number of weeks. It also heard witnesses. However, this is the first time the debate on tax reform will take place in the House. This reform has aroused considerable concern. The Finance Committee alone

July 19, 1988
Income Tax and Related Acts
received more than 400 letters and briefs and heard thirty witnesses from all parts of the country and all levels of our society. What do these Canadians have to say to the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs and to parliamentarians? Basically, they don't like this tax reform. Families don't like it, middle-income taxpayers don't like it, R & D firms don't like it, mining regions are disenchanted, and insurance companies, self-employed workers and farmers came here to explain their dissatisfaction with this legislation.
In fact, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has the satisfaction of getting a unanimous response to his Bill, since everyone agrees it is unacceptable. More specifically, Canadians came to tell the Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs:
First, that the tax reform is merely a smoke screen because it is an attempt to camouflage four years of massive tax and income tax increases.
Second, these people came to tell the Committee that this reform is incomplete because it postpones the most important part, sales tax reform, until after the election.
Third, people came to tell us that this reform does not simplify our taxation system and in many ways makes it more complex.
Fourth, Canadians told us that the reform does not make the tax system more progressive, more equitable or fairer for private citizens.
Fifth, they told us that the reform hits hardest at middle-income taxpayers.
Sixth, the reform is entirely unfair to families.
Seventh, it discourages the building of capital.
Eighth, it makes businesses, especially in the manufacturing and research and development sectors, less competitive.
And ninth, the reform makes life more difficult for selfemployed workers.
But before analyzing this reform in greater detail, Mr. Speaker, I would like to explain the broad principles that should have served as a guide to the tax reform proposed by the Minister of Finance.

The thrust of the Minister's reform centres on removal of incentives from the tax system and lowering of the tax rates. This general thrust, if I may say so at this point, is in sharp contrast to the position the Minister originally took upon coming into office, in his first three Budgets. You will probably remember that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), in his previous Budgets, introduced extremely costly tax incentives such as a capital gains exemption, and on a number of occasions he increased the tax burden, mainly by partially deindexing the tax system and imposing surtaxes. Now the Minister has recognized the error of his ways and has
repented, at least on these issues. This change of heart is a death bed repentance and I do not think Canadians will be fooled by the eleventh hour conversion. The pre-electoral timing is just too blatant.
In these various political games that the Minister of Finance plays he has completely neglected to reach the key objective of tax reform, that is to have a tax system which is equitable, redistributive, and fair. Equity and fairness must be achieved in ways which do not lower work incentives either at the lower or at the upper end of the income scale.
Clearly, this reform has in no way improved the progressivi-ty of the tax system. This has been illustrated vividly by at least three different studies which show that middle-income Canadians are hardest hit by this reform. Those studies were done by the Institute of Research on Public Policy, the Senate Committee on Tax Reform, and the Thorne Ernst Whinney analysis. In other words, this is not real tax reform since it neglects to institute what Canadians value the most, namely fairness.
Concerning the role of incentives in the economy, as a general principle we in the Liberal Party favour a move toward a reduction of incentives. We also favour the use of this new room to manoeuvre to lower the tax rates. Tax incentives, when they are blindly piled up on top of each other, can represent-and I emphasize "can"-an inefficient way of encouraging a type of economic activity. They can also distort progressivity in the personal income tax system and can hide the real cost of those programs.
This general principle, however, has to be balanced against other government policies. For instance, if drilling in the mining sector drops off, or if research and development in Canada lags behind other countries, there are legitimate arguments in favour of tax incentives over other forms of government tools such as direct government grants. Tax incentives tend to reduce the role of government bureaucracies and their ability to make discretionary choices.
Pragmatic as always, Liberals believe that governments should, under certain circumstances, use tax incentives to shift the short-term direction of the economy or to solve structural problems for a better long-term allocation of resources or a fairer balance of economic development among regions and sectors.
One must not minimize the enormous challenges the Canadian economy faces if it is to grow at rates necessary to meet the income and employment demands of our people. We should not underestimate the structural weaknesses of our economy. There seems little doubt that in an economic context where high income countries need to be at the cutting edge in research and development based industries, a strategy based purely on the free market or on foreign-centred firms will not be successful.
July 19, 1988

It is obvious to me, as it is to many business people, that tax reform will not meet this new challenge. It puts our manufacturing sector at a competitive disadvantage. It puts our research and development firms at a disadvantage. It puts our small businesses at a disadvantage. It puts our entrepreneurs, our risk takers, at a disadvantage. Ultimately, this will only reduce growth and jobs.
One way to settle the dilemma that the Government faces by keeping useful tax incentives that run counter to progressivity is to set a limit on the total amount of deductions an individual can claim. A "box" of deductions could, for instance, be set up. An individual would not be allowed to claim more than a certain amount or proportion of his income in regard to that box. This box would be a more effective tool to ensure that every taxpayer pays a fair share of taxes. In other words, it is a minimum tax that can replace the complex and ineffective so-called alternative minimum tax of the Tory Government.
I also think that all new incentives, as well as all the existing ones, should be accompanied by a three to five-year revision clause and be subject to parliamentary scrutiny. I emphasize that I am not speaking here of a sunset clause that would automatically kill an incentive after a given period of time, but of a revision clause.

Mr. Speaker, instead of proceeding with the kind of tax reform I just described, the Minister of Finance, a bit like his Prime Minister, preferred to make this reform a political game. For instance, in a pre-election move that did not deceive anyone, the Government announced that as of July 1988, the tax reform would result in a slight drop in source deductions on the paychecks of many taxpayers. Whatever the Mulroney Government cares to think, this respite is merely a smoke screen, a pre-election move to make us forget four years of tax increases unprecedented in this country's history.
The tax reform as tabled is merely the latest in a series of increases in personal income tax, sales tax and excise tax. If we look at studies made by independent agencies, the tax measures introduced by the Conservative Government in the past four years have been both regressive and unfair.
In a report published recently, the Institute for Research on Public Policy calculated the impact on the taxpayer of all changes in personal income tax made by the Conservatives since they came to power. To those figures we must add the additional burden on taxpayers as a result of numerous increases in indirect taxes, such as the increase in federal sales tax from 9 to 12 per cent and the 5 cent per litre increase in the excise tax on gas. There are three points one can make as a result of these calculations, and I would say, Mr. Speaker, that these three points reflect the main deficiencies of the tax reform proposed in Bill C-139 before the House today.
First, in 1988, even after the tax reform, all taxpayers will pay more income tax then they did in 1984, with one exception: taxpayers with an income exceeding $117,000 a year. The
Income Tax and Related Acts
average tax saving for this privileged group, which represents only 1 per cent of Canadian families, is about $3,500 annually.
Mr. Speaker, this means that all taxpayers will pay more income tax except those privileged members of our society with an annual income of more than $117,000.
Second, middle-income families, for instance a family with an annual income of $32,000, will pay $1,200 more in taxes than in 1984.
On this side of the House, when we talk about the unfairness of the Conservative Government's tax reform, the following example is eloquent. The rich, people with an annual income of $117,000 or more, stand to gain over $3,500 per year as a result of the tax reform, while middle-income families with children will pay an additional $1,200 per year.
If we look at the federal Government's total revenues, if we consider the projections made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his last Budget, and we compare these with the Government's revenue in 1984-85, we realize that corporate income tax increased by only 28 per cent, while personal income tax, including sales tax and excise tax, has increased by 62 per cent, which means 62 per cent more for workers and only 28 per cent more for corporations.
In other words, Canadians will not be fooled by the Government's attempt to gloss over four years of massive tax increases, which took place despite promises made to the Canadian people by the present Minister of Finance and the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when they were campaigning in September 1984.
So despite promises by the present Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that they would not increase taxes, the list of tax increases has grown steadily in the past four years.
Mr. Speaker, I shall mention the main increases. First of all, federal sales tax has increased by 3 per cent: from 9 per cent to 10 per cent in October 1984, just after this Government was elected, and then to 11 per cent on January 1, 1986, and to 12 per cent on April 1, 1986.
This decision by the Finance Minister and the Conservative Government means that just on the basis of these rate increases, in 1988 Canadians are going to pay over $3 billion more in sales tax.
Mr. Speaker, sales tax was extended to candy, soft drinks, health care products and dental instruments on July 1, 1985, which brought in an additional $400 million. All candy and snacks were taxed, which raised $60 million more for the Government, on an annual basis.
The sales tax on paint, wallpaper and toys was increased from 8 to 12 per cent. The excise tax on gas was increased four times, Mr. Speaker. First, two cents a litre more on September 3, 1985, then one cent per litre more on January 1, 1987, another cent on Febuary 17, and another cent again on April 1, 1988. This adds up to a total of 5 cents a litre or more than 23 cents a gallon. The sales tax on leaded gas was raised to

July 19, 1988
Income Tax and Related Acts
bring the price to the same level as that of unleaded gas. There was a progressive increase in the air transportation tax, and excise tax and duties on alcohol and tobacco were increased four times between May 24, 1985 and January 1, 1988. Mr. Speaker, one tax I find outrageous is the 10 per cent tax on long distance calls which became effective on January 1, 1988. The hardest hit are those living in remote areas who must call long distance to reach their doctor, their accountant, their general store, and so forth. This tax will raise an additional one billion dollars and will have a negative impact on regional development across this country. These tax increases were all introduced by the Conservative government since 1984.
And what about income tax? First, the tax tables were partially de-indexed, which increased the tax burden on Canadian families by $635 million then and there. Since the $635 million applies to the first year, January 1986, it means that in 1987, it was twice that and in 1988, three times, Mr. Speaker. This means that in 1988, Canadian taxpayers are paying over two billion dollars more in income tax because of the Finance Minister's decision.
Tax exemptions have been eliminated: $650 million. The deduction for registered home ownership savings plans was eliminated $100 million. The temporary 5 per cent and 10 per cent surtax and then the general permanent surtax of 3 per cent were introduced. Changes were made in the tax treatment of dividends. Married exemptions were changed. Mr. Speaker, all these tax increases were introduced by a Government that made a solemn promise to Canadians that it would not increase taxes.
If we add it all up, Mr. Speaker, you know how much this represents? It works out to $26.7 billion in new taxes, for a Government that promised not to increase taxes for Canadian taxpayers. And when after that they tell us, as the Finance Minister did last week, that the deficit will be $28 billion instead of $29 billion, what kind of an attitude is that on the part of a Finance Minister who just increased taxes by $26 billion! And pleased as punch because he managed to reduce his deficit by $1 billion!
Mr. Speaker, I will get back later to the deficit. For some days now, in fact some weeks, billions of dollars have been spent left and right. Have we had a progress report from the Minister of Finance? How can this Government give away billions and billions of dollars without ever giving the House a statement of revenues and expenditures for the next five years? It's easy, Mr. Speaker. Every time they give away another billion, they charge it to future budgets so that the current year is not affected. The following year will be marginally affected but later on, the bills will start coming in, and then this Government which is so proud of reducing its deficit will have to come clean or take the consequences.
As a result of those measures, "tax freedom day" as calculated by the Fraser Institute has occurred later and later each year since 1984. It now occurs on July 10, which means that the average family works more than six months just to pay its federal, provincial and local, direct and indirect, visible and hidden taxes. The Government has done nothing to reverse this trend. At least these taxes could be collected fairly, but unfortunately that has not been the case. Furthermore, this is only current taxation.
If one considers that the deficits are nothing else but deferred taxation, the average taxpayer will work from January 1 to August 12 merely to pay taxes.

The answer to this question: Why has the Government done nothing? I will say, Mr. Speaker, that when you look at the tax increases brought in by this Government, when you look at what has happened over the last few years, you see that this Government is just deceiving the Canadian electorate.

In spite of these numerous tax increases, public finances remain extremely vulnerable to any downturn in the economy. The Government brags of its success in reducing the deficit, but the reality is that it has not prepared the Canadian economy for the inevitable downturn which many economists fear will come as early as next year.
In spite of six years of strong growth, thanks to the global economic picture, and in spite of four years of massive tax increases, the deficit is still in the $28 billion-$29 billion range. The public debt now amounts to more than $320 billion, or more than $25,000 per taxpayer.

Mr. Speaker, we also know that tax reform will be done in stages. The first step took effect on January 1, 1988 and contains a few tax reductions but unfortunately its impact was not felt on pay cheques until the beginning of July. Six months later! Why? The answer to this question is obvious: this Government acts only in response to political pressure. July 1 was chosen because it was near the elections, so that voters could feel a slight tax decrease after being hit with $26 billion in increases; the Government gives a few billion back and does it on July 1 to make it as close as it can to a possible election date. And in order to keep some room to manoeuvre, to be able to play on all fronts, the Government said to itself that with the July 1 date, if it could not hold the elections in 1988 but only in the spring of 1989, the refund for the first six months of 1988 would be paid then. It will give the voters another small gift and hope to buy their votes with their own money. Mr. Speaker, this is a loan of over one billion dollars that the Government has given itself. Many Canadians and companies would like to be able to give themselves the same privilege of interest-free loans.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a few minutes in this speech to denounce the other election trick of the Government, namely announcing now the good news, or what it claims to be good news, but leaving the bad news for after the election. I wish to talk about this two-stage reform and the one that is not on the legislative agenda now, sales tax reform. The Government is waiting until after the elections to bring it in. It is clear that the Government is only trying to repeat the trick it pulled in 1984. This Government then promised not to increase taxes. And we know how much this Government has increased taxes since 1984! Today they are trying to give us the good news before the elections, but after, watch out! That is when this famous sales tax will hit us. They did not want to introduce it in one step, as all observers and all Canadians who came to the Finance and Economic Affairs Committee asked, so that they could see the pros and cons and know what to expect for the future...
But this Government lacked courage! We must recall that more than three years ago, the most important component of tax reform according to this Minister of Finance was sales tax reform.
So much so, Mr. Speaker, that at that point the Minister of Finance did not even refer to personal income tax reform-he only stressed sales tax reform. He even suggested the existing sales tax, to use his own words, was "a silent killer of jobs".
He also indicated, as the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Hockin) yesterday repeated in his speech, the sales tax was hurting exports, and helping imports, in addition to being excessively complex to administer.
Income Tax and Related Acts
And so, may I ask, if since 1985 that tax has had so many flaws, how come the only part of the tax system that has not now been reformed is the sales tax?
Mr. Speaker, the C.D. Howe Institute even indicated in its 1988 report titled "Focus on follow through", the major economic advantages to be derived from reforming our tax system would come from reforming the sales tax rather than direct taxes. But when the time came to proceed with that reform, this Minister and this Government backed off.
Mr. Speaker, we in the Liberal Party feel that the current sales tax system must be improved. The Liberal Party is committed to reforming that tax upon coming to power. We further feel that basic foods such as milk, bread, butter and meat, should be non taxable items.
Moreover, we believe that a generous refundable tax credit must be established, to be indexed and paid in installments to middle and low income families.
Mr. Speaker, let me now say a few words concerning the complexity of that tax reform included in Bill C-139. I must first emphasize that the legislation includes more than 500 pages, 500 pages without even an index. Try and find your way through that!
In those more than 500 pages of text, there are a number of explanatory notes. We might as well laugh rather than weep over that! Especially when one of the major objectives announced by the Minister was to simplify the tax law.
To sum up my views on the matter, that reform no doubt is one of the most complex we have ever seen in this House. The tax system is being made much more complex in a number of areas rather than simpler. Even the experts can hardly find their way through that maze.
It should be remembered that in October 1986, the Minister of Finance stated in the document titled Guidelines for tax reform in Canada that one of the objectives was, and I quote: "making the tax system simpler so that it is more readily understood by more Canadians".
Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing all observers agree on, it is that the simplification goal never was achieved.

The best example that has been given to us concerning the complexity of tax reform has been provided by the Joint Committee on Taxation of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. Let me quote what it said in its May 1988 submission about the so-called simplification:
Our review and analysis of the April draft legislation, (now Bill C-139), only reinforced the conviction of the Joint Committee, that if simplification was a priority objective of the tax reform process, the Government has failed.

July 19, 1988

The most important consequence of such a complexity is, in the words of the Joint Committee, "the prospect of widespread non-compliance".
The report of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs on tax reform came to the same conclusion. It capped its chapter on tax simplification by saying: "Tax reform has not successfully addressed the problem of simplifying the tax system". Why did the Minister promise something when he had no intention of delivering?

According to a recent study conducted for the Canadian Tax Fondation, only 30 per cent of taxpayers are brave enough to complete their income tax returns themselves. Nearly 40 per cent have it done by specialized firms, and 30 per cent by friends or relatives. If such was the case under the previous tax law, my prediction is a still larger proportion of Canadians will have to use tax experts in order to complete their income tax returns that otherwise could be greatly simplified.

I recognize that tax simplification is not an easy thing to achieve. It is a long-term goal. However, to achieve any progress at all, I believe, again with the Joint Committee, that the Government must make a firm commitment to simplification as a priority and be willing to accept trade-offs with other policy objectives.
If you remember, Mr. Speaker, in June 1986, the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs released a report about tax simplification. I must point out that this was a unanimous report also signed by the majority of the Conservative members of the committee. Those recommendations called for measures to simplify both the income tax form, which is the key aspect of tax simplification for most taxpayers, and the Tax Act itself. The Government should have acted but it did not. Why? Liberals have always stressed the importance of having a progressive tax system. It is a question of equity and fairness. No other issue more naturally divides Conservatives from Liberals. I fear that income distribution has worsened over the last four years. This is partly a result of economic trends, but also because of a tax system which has become much less progressive.
I believe one of the most important ways to redistribute wealth in this country is the tax system. What the Tories have done is to redistribute the revenue, but upside down, giving more money to the rich and taking more from the middle-class and lower-income earners. Along with millions of Canadians, I am shocked to see that every taxpayer pays more taxes in 1988, even after tax reform, than in 1984, except those earning more than $117,000 a year. I am shocked that some 60,000 profitable corporations will continue not to pay any tax despite tax reform, and I am also shocked at some 5,220 taxpayers with incomes above $50,000 a year paid no tax in 1986. Forty of those have incomes of over $250,000 a year.
You have to remember, Mr. Speaker, that 1986 was the first year of the implementation of the so-called minimum tax by the Tory Government. That is not fairness. It is not progress-ivity. Even though those numbers are striking, the most perniciously regressive aspect of tax reform is to be found in the new tax structure with three levels. It is not easy to explain why this new structure lacks progressivity, but the difficulty of the task does not make the system acceptable.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the number of tax rates have been reduced from ten to three. We now have three rates, 17 per cent, 26 per cent and 29 per cent. These are the federal rates only. Provincial rates must be added to these rates. Have you ever asked yourself, Mr. Speaker, why the 26 per cent rate, which kicks in at $27,500, is so near to the 29 per cent rate paid by high-income earners? Why is it that the 26 per cent rate, which is the middle rate, does not lie right in the middle between 17 per cent and 29 per cent? The answer to this question is very simple. The Government has decided to raise the middle rate to 26 per cent because it did not proceed with the reform of the sales tax immediately. This is why the Government claims that under phase 2 of the tax reform, when the sales tax will be reformed, enough revenue will be generated to reduce the middle rate. This is an implicit recognition by the Government of the unfairness of its new tax structure.
Those who are hurt are middle-income earners. Those with incomes between $30,000, $40,000 and $45,000 a year are the big losers with tax reform, and the Government knows it. What we used to call the silent majority are people earning between $30,000 and $45,000. The Government hits that group because it knows that those people will not come here to Parliament Hill and demonstrate their disapproval. However, I am confident they will do so during the time of the next election.
But the situation is even worse than what I have just described. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, in their tax reform report the Senate Committee on Banking, Trade and Commerce pointed out that, on all additional income, a good many middle income families will pay a higher tax rate than will high income households. Mr. Speaker, at the 26 per cent official federal rate a middle income family has to allow for an additional hidden 5 per cent levy due to the fact that every time a family gets a salary increase-say going from $30,000 to $31,000-it stands to lose 5 per cent of its refundable child tax credit. Let us look at it this way: a $30,000-a-year family whose income increases to $31,000 will have to pay a 31 per cent federal tax on the extra $1,000, which is more than the 29 per cent rate a taxpayer whose earnings go up from $100,000 to $101,000 would have to part with. The extra $1,000 in the hands of a family will be taxed at the rate of 31 per cent.

This simple distinction between a common-law and a legal union entails very heavy financial consequences for couples, so much so that in some cases a common-law arrangement is a much better proposition than marriage when it comes to income tax considerations. Many groups gave strong evidence to that effect, but the fact remains that family needs are exactly the same whether the couple are legally married or live as common-law man and wife. First and foremost, I should think, overhauling the family tax system would be the fair approach. Some people might be concerned that such changes would favour a lifestyle over another, but not so, Mr. Speaker. I think that the state must avoid making a value judgment on the kind of union it prefers, it has to respect personal choices and give fair treatment to all couples no matter what their lifestyle may be. That was the low-key message conveyed by the Standing Committee on Human Rights. So what has the Minister of Finance been doing to make tax legislation more consistent with our society's changing mores? Not a thing, Mr. Speaker!

The Finance Committee has recognized this problem of capital taxation, and has proposed many measures to improve the situation. As the Senate committee report said, the question of capital taxation and of taxation of investment income has to be thoroughly reviewed. The Government must generate a new set of proposals more favourable to investments in the country's long-term competitive needs. The Liberal Party recognized this need.

Mr. Speaker, I did not have time in the 40 minutes allotted to me to deal with all aspects of tax reform. For example, I leave it to my colleagues from Outremont (Mrs. Pepin) and Trinity (Miss Nicholson) to go further into the taxation of families, especially children. I leave it to my colleagues from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) and Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) to discuss the issues relating to seniors.

I did not have time to go to the bottom of the questions affecting research and development, and taxation of farmers. Neither did I have time to develop many other aspects concerning small business, taxation of... for example, the whole question of car expenses and offices at home. These are all questions that I hope my colleagues will deal with.
I did not have time either to talk about the taxation of insurance companies, which will have a considerable impact on Canadians' savings in those institutions. I did not have time to discuss the taxation rate of small manufacturing companies. The Minister had promised to lower the tax rate for small business from 10 to 8 per cent. Despite that, he increased it to 12 per cent. Neither do I have time to talk about the film industry.

This tax reform is only a smoke-screen. It remains incomplete; it does not simplify the tax system; it in no way improves the progressiveness or equity of the tax system; it places an unfair burden on middle-income Canadians; it is unjust for families; it discourages capitalization; it reduces the competitiveness of businesses; it makes life difficult for the selfemployed.
The net result of Bill C-139 is that, in 1988, even after tax reform, all taxpayers will pay more taxes than in 1984 with the exception of those privileged few whose income is $117,000 and over. The average reduction in taxes for this group, which represents a mere 1 per cent of Canadians families, is close to $3,500. Second, a family with two children earning $32,000 a year will see their taxes increase by an average of $1,200 in comparison to 1984. Finally, if we compare the total revenues of the federal Government between 1988-89 and 1984-85, we realize that corporation tax increased by 28 per cent, while personal taxes and sales and excise taxes, paid for by all Canadians, increased by 62 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak specifically about Bill C-139 which deals with the Government's tax reform. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) talked about a sense of urgency with respect to this Bill. It is interesting to me that this sense of urgency was such that the Government brought its tax proposals forward last June after lengthy delays, and then in December it decided what it was going to do. It was not until June 30 of this year that it finally tabled its tax reform proposals.
What came forward was not tax reform in the sense of a fairness that people were looking for across the country. What we got was Tory tax reform. This means that the interests of wealthy Canadians and of corporations was put ahead of the interests of average Canadians.
That is indicated by such facts as the following. The biggest tax cut in the tax reform is the cut in corporate tax rates from 36 per cent to 28 per cent. The biggest beneficiaries in terms of the income earners who win from this are wealthy Canadians earning over $100,000 per year. Average Canadians get about $6 per week in tax cuts. They have had far more than that in tax increases over the course of the last four years since the Conservatives came to power just under four years ago. But wealthy Canadians get an average of some $80 per week. What that means is that it is lunch at Winston's every week for a wealthy Canadian family which gets tax cuts under this particular tax reform, but for the average Canadian it is two big Macs and one milkshake to share every week.
July 19, 1988

The Bill which has come forward is some 500 pages long. It is an abuse of Parliament for the Government now to have this Bill before Parliament and the people of Canada for as short a period of time as the Government intends to have it.
The Finance Committee has worked at this Bill with a great deal of energy and effectiveness. Despite the fact that we disagreed about basic issues such as progressivity, nonetheless we made a large number of very useful and constructive proposals. I regret the fact that, perhaps guided by the Finance Department, or perhaps guided by its own ideological motivation, the Government has systematically chosen to ignore the vast bulk of those recommendations, let alone the recommendations coming from the New Democratic Party.
I want to serve notice to the Minister of State for Finance, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and to all members of the Conservative Party that tax reform will be a major issue in the forthcoming general election campaign. The options that Canadians will have to choose will be between Tory tax reform that benefits the rich and the corporations on the one hand and fair tax reform as proposed by my leader and the New Democrats on the other hand and what we have been fighting for over the last many years.
What the Government has done is to put forward changes in the tax system to please its friends in the business community and among wealthy communities. I would say to the Minister of State for Finance that a symbol of the Conservative priorities is the fact that the urgency of tax reform that they saw was a tax-free capital gains provision of half a million dollars for wealthy Canadians most of whom earn more than $100,000 per year. As a symbol of the Tory priorities, when the Prime Minister had to replace his Principal Secretary, did he choose a union leader? Did he choose someone who had worked with the poor? Did he choose a woman who knows the problems that women have in having second class citizenship in our society? No, no, and no.
Who did he choose? The Prime Minister chose a close associate of Conrad Black of Argus Corporation. He brought the corporate elite to the Prime Minister's Office by putting Peter White to work as his Principal Secretary. That indicates the priorities of this particular Government.
The average Canadian has had tax increases on an average income of about $1,300 per year since 1984. That is the reality of Conservative tax policy. Under tax reform, if they are lucky they will get a tax cut of about $300 per year. That means that for every $4 that they have had taken from them in tax increases they will get $1 back. The finance critic from the Liberal Party tried to suggest that the Liberal Party was opposed to the approach to taxation taken by the Progressive Conservatives. He seems to have a short memory. Perhaps because he just came to the House only in 1984.
Who was it that began all the tax concessions to wealthy corporations? It was the Liberal Party. Who was it that began the cuts in top tax rates which are being continued by the

Progressive Conservatives? It was the Liberal Party. Who was it that began the increases in sales tax?

The sales tax increases which had been first initiated by the Liberal Party were later on perpetuated by the Tory Party. Which is the party which widened the sales tax base to make sure that an increasing number of consumer goods used by the middle income Canadian family would be taxed? It is the Liberal Party which started all that, Mr. Speaker. Which is the Party which was the first to impose taxes on Canadian families below the poverty line? It is again the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker. Who started the de-indexing process? It is the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker, with the 6 p. 100 and 5 p. 100 program which it introduced in the early 1980's. Who has maintained the archaic sales tax system which still exists now? It is again the Liberal Party which did nothing to change the system.
Who used its empty rhetoric to defend the fairness of the tax system? It is the Liberal Party, followed now by the Tory Party. That is why I wonder if the Liberal Party would increase the taxes on major corporations? The Liberals are like the Tories. They would equally preserve the privileges of the private industry in our country, just as they did when they were in Government. That is why I urge Canadians to judge the two major parties on their deeds rather than on their words, to judge the Liberal Party on what it achieved while in Government. When they sit on this side of the House, the Liberals talk like New Democrats, but when they are in Government, they act like Conservatives.

They talk like New Democrats when they are in opposition, but they act like Conservatives when they are in government. That is why when we say that tax reform will be a major issue in the forthcoming election campaign and New Democrats will be talking about fairness in taxation for average Canadians. We will put our proposals up against those of the Conservatives. We will put our proposals up against those of the Liberals as well. We will contrast the kind of fairness that we are talking about with what the Conservatives are doing in office and with what the Liberals did when they had power just a few short years ago.
It is interesting to recall that from 1981 to 1984 when the Liberals were in power Canada's banks with profits of more than $5 billion paid approximately 2 per cent of those profits in tax-about $72 million. Canada's trust and life insurance companies paid around 5 per cent of their profits in federal income tax.
It is interesting to note that during that period of time a teller in a branch of the Royal Bank paid more in tax than the Royal Bank itself paid. Did we hear the finance critic from the Liberal Party, who was then himself a bank president, criticize that particular position? He was silent. Did we hear Liberal back-benchers criticize that particular situation? They were silent. Did we hear Conservatives in opposition criticize that

situation? They were silent as well. Yet that is a situation which creates unfairness, cynicism and, finally, non-compliance from average Canadians who say: "Look, if the big corporations are getting all of the breaks, why the devil shouldn't I fiddle my taxes just a little bit as well?"
That is fundamentally demoralizing and undermining to the tax system which depends on voluntary compliance. If Canadians were really looking for fairness and frankness from the tax reform, then they are disappointed and will be disappointed with what they get from the Conservatives. In terms of fairness, when all is said and done what the Conservative tax reform really means is that three out of four wealthy families earning over $100,000 per year will get an average $4,165 per year in tax cuts.
Where does that figure come from? It does not come from the researchers in the NDP, it does not come from a bunch of gnomes in the back room of our Party who devised that. It is in the Government's own documents. The Government itself admits that after its tax reforms, some 60,000 profitable Canadian corporations will continue to get off every year without paying any tax. In addition to that, the Conservatives have been hardly frank with the Canadian people. They have kept the bad news hidden in terms of what they intend to do about the new sales tax. The Democrats admit and accept that we need a change in the present sales tax system. It is up to the Government to act on this issue. The Finance Committee has just in fact come back with a report indicating that the current changes, the interim changes proposed by the Government on sales tax, are unworkable, unacceptable and ineffective, but we do not know what the Government intends to do.
It was only after months of pressure that we finally had the Minister of Finance accepting that he was not going to continue with his long-cherished ambition to slap an 8 or 10 per cent sales tax on food, on the groceries that every Canadian buys every week. Now, we just do not know what else will be taxed and what is out. The Minister of State for Finance is here. He can interrupt me now and tell me what is going to be taxed and what is not, what is in and what is out. How much will any tax cuts that took effect in July of this year for average families be wiped out once we have the regressive sales tax as proposed by a Conservative Government that puts the interests of the wealthy and of corporations first? How will that affect the tax savings?

speechtext:
The Conservatives may have got some of the ingredients right, but they are still following the same recipe that favours the wealthy and lets the largest corporations off easy. The end result is that the average Canadian family is left paying the bill.
Let me point out that three out of four wealthy families get over $4,000 a year in tax cut. The average family earning $35,000 a year gets a cut of only $350 a year. The family earning under $15,000 a year gets a cut of only $100 a year.
In addition to that, the tax reform as proposed by the Conservatives is fundamentally unfair when it comes to families across Canada. As far as families are concerned, the Conservatives think that all it takes to raise a family is $65 a year in tax credit, over and above what is given to the tax system for the average taxpayer who is single. It is $65 a year per child. It is a bit more for the third and subsequent child, if your income is under $24,000 a year. But a tax credit of $65 a year is about $1.28 per week, I believe. Now, $1.28 per week, I would like to inform the Minister of State for Finance, will not even buy one of the cheapest hamburgers at McDonald's or at Burger King in order to help that kid make it through the week. Certainly, it will not pay for the food, milk, extra housekeeping, clothing, personal supplies, educational supplies, sporting goods that a child needs, if the child is going to live normally with his or her peers, for all of the other expenses that are entailed in having children and raising kids.
I think people have said that raising a child these days is an investment which we carefully make. It may be $75,000 or $90,000 over the childhood of that child, until the child is independent and on his own at the age of 20 or 21.
What does a Conservative Party propose to give in terms of that cost? Well, $65 over 20 years works out to about $1,300 or perhaps 1 per cent of the extra cost to families who are raising kids.
Finally, the Conservatives point out that 850,000 taxpayers will be taken off the tax rolls, but they ignore the dimension. A million taxpayers have been added to the tax rolls since 1984. If the wealthy had paid their fair share under the tax system as proposed by the Progressive Conservatives, middle and low-income families could have got a fairer tax break. If the wealthy had paid their fair share, we could have taken families which were below the poverty line off the tax rolls in terms of paying income tax, instead of a family who is $1,000 below the poverty line paying tax. A family who is $2,000 below the poverty line will be paying federal income tax. A family who is $3,000 below will be paying tax. In fact, the tax for families will begin at around $18,500. The poverty line in urban Canada, for an urban Canadian family right now is some $23,000 per annum. So you reach down to $4,500 below the
July 19, 1988

poverty line and yet people at that level are still going to be paying tax.
It is interesting to note what the priorities of this Government are. A taxpayer with an income of $30,000 a year, if he or she is single, will get a $695 tax cut. The Minister nods. He acknowledges the figures which are drawn from his figure. A single taxpayer earner with two kids, with a spouse who is not working, will get a tax reduction of $590. If it is a more typical Canadian family, two income earners and two kids under 18, it will get a tax cut of $285. A single person over 65 will get a cut of $430.
It is significant that in the typical Canadian family with two incomes it takes two wage earners to support the kids, pay the mortgage or the rent, and buy the food and other essentials that you need. That particular family at $30,000 a year, instead of getting the largest tax cut-which would seem to make sense-gets the smallest tax cut, while the single person gets the largest cut. There is something fundamentally wrong about that.
We, the New Democrats, believe that the Canadian tax system is long overdue for fundamental reform. We stand out and speak up for fairness, efficiency and simplicity in the tax system, but the tax system that we have in Bill C-139 is neither fair, efficient nor simple. The committee has come in with some useful suggestions, but it failed to take up the challenge of redrafting the proposal in terms of the fundamental principles which should underpin real tax reform.
Let me cite one specific thing. The first recommendation of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, I regret to say, was to endorse the rate structure which is contained in the proposals put forward under tax reform by the Minister and by the Government. I think it was a very serious mistake because, when you cut the top rate of taxation from some 34 per cent of the federal level down to 29 per cent, it is impossible to create a progressive tax system. When you create a situation where a secretary working for Bell Canada pays a marginal rate of tax, only five points less than the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Bell Canada, Mr. Jean de Grandpre, who has an income of close to one million dollars a year, there is something fundamentally wrong with that. Average Canadians will tell you that, and yet, somehow the Government is so distant from average Canadians that it simply does not understand that at all.
How can you defend a situation where out of every dollar that Mr. de Grandpre gets in additional income he pays only a nickel more in tax than the secretary who perhaps is trying to raise a couple of kids and live on her own, perhaps on one income, and certainly is having a tough time getting by on that particular income?
While the tax system's intention is, among other things, to raise funds for government expenditures, it is also a serious moral and philosophical intervention into the society and the economy. We live in a society where income is unequally distributed through the mechanism of the market in the form
Income Tax and Related Acts
of wages, salaries, dividends, interest and that kind of thing. Income is not distributed equally and the market will not distribute it equally. Whether or not the market acts efficiently in economic growth, it is a poor instrument for realizing social equity. Therefore, as New Democrats, we believe that the central focus of the tax system is to achieve a redistribution of income from the wealthy to average and lower-income Canadians. What the Conservatives believe is something completely contrary. They have been captured by the neoConservative view that we need to get the tax system down to a system of taxation as flat as possible. If they could have reduced the categories from 10 rates to 1 rather than 10 rates to 3, I believe they would have done so if they felt they could have sold that, but in the end they could not do that.
The Conservatives are setting the stage for a shift from income taxation over to consumption taxes, despite the fact that consumption taxes affect average Canadians much more than they affect wealthy Canadians, because wealthy Canadians can afford to defer expenditure and consumption because they have lots of money to go around. The Conservatives are creating a system which is less and less progressive. That is demonstrated by the fact that the biggest tax cuts go to wealthy Canadians and the smallest tax cuts go to average Canadians.
The reform package here fails to achieve any substantial redistribution of income among Canadians. The one progressive part of the system, which is the personal income tax, is not far from being neutral in its impact. The reform package is consciously structured so as to be neutral in terms of income distribution. Otherwise progressive features, such as converting tax exemptions which favour upper income earners to tax credits which favour lower income earners are more than offset to changes to the structure of tax rates.
If you really believe in fairness, Mr. Speaker, then you would judge that all forms of income should be treated equally. The Liberals, however, do not believe in fairness. When they were in power they did not treat income equally, and the Conservatives are no better. Income from property, such as capital gains and dividends, is treated differently by the Conservatives than income from wages and salaries.
I hear the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Bosley) basically supporting the privilege in which many of his constituents live since he comes from one of the most affluent constituencies in the country. While I have great respect for the Hon. Member, who is a former Speaker and a distinguished Member of this House of Commons, I want to suggest to him that his constituents are far less in need, and if they are committed to a fair society here, they should be prepared to accept willingly a redistribution of income through the tax system rather than fighting at the top always to be in first place.

Income Tax and Related Acts
I go on to point out that we think the corporate share of the over-all tax burden which represents a withholding tax on property income should be increased. We think that the sales tax share, which represents a regressive tax on consumers, should be reduced. Unfortunately, this question of balance was not examined at any length by the Finance Committee nor, of course, was it examined to any extent by the Government.
We think as well that there is a real problem in tax fairness between big business and small businesses in Canada. That continues in the tax reform which is here. The tax rate on businesses and on larger corporations is alleged to rise by a modest amount. The corporate share of Canadian tax collections, which was about 20 per cent in 1984 when the Conservatives came to power, is down to 15 per cent today. In four or five years time it will still be no more than abut 17 per cent of total tax collections, about $1 in every $6, whereas the average taxpayers will be paying well over half of those tax collections, Mr. Speaker. In addition to that, tax benefits intended to create jobs are overwhelmingly concentrated and directed toward large corporations, while small businesses pay more tax and yet create the vast majority of new jobs in this country.
I would say that if we are talking about efficiency, and that is an important goal as well, then the Government has failed to come to grips with the whole question of tax expenditures, which amount to some $30 billion a year, which amount to a sum equal or greater than the annual sum of the deficit in Canada, and which the Government has simply not touched through the tax reform. If you were to take these tax expenditures and reviewed and assessed them on an annual basis, as the New Democrats believe should be done, then you would start to create a system that would be more efficient, you would be measuring every expenditure by a Government whether it was a direct expenditure or an expenditure through the tax system.

Unfortunately, the Tory Government has done nothing in that direction. We believe it is possible to target tax expenditures to ensure that key objectives such as job creation and regional development are achieved with considerably less spending on the Government's part. Once in a while, some tax expenditures are justified such as the flow-through shares. Nevertheless, we believe that in a great many cases, direct expenditures from the Government are much more efficient than tax expenditures to reach national economic goals.

We believe that the goal of accountability has not been seriously addressed by the Government or by the committee. That is what I was saying just now. We recommend that each tax expenditure program should be assigned to a relevant Department for review and consideration every year with regard to alternative policy instruments.
We believe that there should be a tax expenditure analysis presented annually, along with the spending Estimates, the
Budget and the Public Accounts. We believe the tax expenditures should be integrated with the spending envelope system and be subjected to the approval of Parliament. Unfortunately, we are not making much progress on that. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because wealthy Canadians and corporate Canada know they have a better chance of making headway through the back door via tax expenditures than through the front door via direct expenditure by Government.
Finally, on this front, we have the question of simplicity. The Bill which is 500 pages long hardly adds to simplicity. In fact, the tax practitioners are absolutely beside themselves in trying to deal with this tax measure. I regret that the measure is likely to go through the committee and back through this House with little or no effective scrutiny of the details of the legislation.
In 1986, before tax reform, half of all Canadians had someone else prepare their tax returns. One-third of Canadians had tax experts prepare their tax returns because they were too complex for them. Ordinary Canadians are increasingly baffled by the complexity of the tax system. That will certainly not change through this provision. In fact, that is also true as far as corporations are concerned.
There has been a lot of talk about the automobile expense provisions which the committee urged be fundamentally changed and which advice the Government ignored. I read through a seven page memo prepared by one of the leading accounting firms that purported to explain the new provisions on automobile expenses. I have to confess that I did not understand it, even as someone who has some expertise in this area and who has spent the last year looking at tax reform as a member of the Finance Committee. If I cannot understand it, how can someone who is running a small business understand it? How can a salesperson or someone working for a firm understand it? Why do we have to create a system where every time you turn around you have to resort to a tax lawyer who charges $200 an hour for his or her advice?
We had hoped to see a fairer balance between individuals in the tax system. Unfortunately, that is not to be. We had hoped to see a higher top rate on those people earning $50,000 or $60,000 a year who can afford to make that kind of contribution. We had looked for a system where wealthy Canadians would pay more rather than less.
We are fundamentally in disagreement with the approach taken by the Government, which is to say that it will plug loopholes on the one hand but then turn around and take money which is gained from loopholes and give it back to the same people. When a Department is forced to give up expenditure because of cut-backs in a particular area, it is not allowed to take the money and put it into some other area of Government. The money goes back into the Treasury and is then spent according to the general priorities of the Government. When it comes to tax reform, the Government has shovelled money around so that wealthy Canadians who lost certain loopholes are getting the money back through lower tax rates.

It may be a more neutral tax system, but it is not a tax system that is fair or more equitable.
It should also be noted that the new credits to be introduced in 1988 will not be fully indexed to inflation. The income tax burden on average families will increase in real terms and many more poor families will be forced back on the tax rolls. In other words, the 800,000 families who may be taken off the tax rolls today will find themselves back on them in the unlikely event that this Government is back in power for the next three or four years after the election.
The partial deindexation means that the $300 tax cut for the average family will be systematically eroded to the point where there will be no effective tax cut about three or four years down the line. That is primarily rooted in two things. The first is the failure of the tax reform White Paper to introduce a fair tax rate structure. The second is the failure of the Government to bring in full indexing on tax rates, particularly for people earning under $30,000 a year. Instead, the credits and everything else are partly deindexed as part of the Tory approach to tax reform.
There are other problems and disparities. One is the fact that the Government is still backing away from full taxation of capital gains. My Party disagrees with that. We disagree with the priority given to the $500,000 tax exemption. The fact that it has been capped at $100,000 is modest progress, but the tax exemption should not have been put there in the first place. It should not be changed or maintained, it should be taken out. We think that the principle that a buck is a buck is a buck, first enunciated by the Carter Commission on taxes back in the 1960s, should be endorsed now if we are to keep our country economically strong and provide for economic regional development. Surely people should know that a dollar they earn is taxed on the same basis as for everyone else and there are not sharpsters and wise boys and girls and people who have the inside track who are able to cut their taxes by means of such devices as the privileged rate given to dividends and capital gains.
That is why my Party recommends that, with the exception of farmers and small businesses-

We note that while many of the tax exemptions or deductions in the system have been replaced by credits, at the same time other personal tax measures which largely favoured the

wealthy, such as the deduction for RRSP contributions, the special treatment of dividend income, and the full deduction of interest costs for income, have been treated as deductions rather than credits. If you want a system that deals fairly with people at different income levels, we propose that those be dealt with in the form of a credit rather than a deduction. Why should wealthy Canadians get deductions and average Canadians get credits? Why not make it all a system of credits?
I have already spoken about the unfairness of the system with respect to families. I have spoken about the fact that the tax reductions for average families are themselves derisory. A few bucks a week, and that money is going to be very quickly taken away. They are far less than the tax increases which have taken effect under the Conservatives since 1984.
The figures are a bit difficult to calculate, but the National Council on Welfare calculates that by 1991 the total child benefits for a two-child family at the poverty line will have been reduced by $314, and the average two-child family will actually lose $925. Those figures may have changed a little bit with the changes to the proposals since 1987, but not a heck of a lot. I ask, what kind of country is this when the tax system deals so unfairly with people who are performing, apart from everything else, the one absolutely fundamental responsibility of every generation in any society, which is to ensure that children are born and a new generation comes along to carry the torch and keep the human race going? How do we treat that in Canada? Judging by the Tory tax reform, we treat it with contempt.
We urge that the $65 tax credit per child be significantly increased and indexed to inflation. The change just for the third child and subsequent children is not good enough. We believe the new credit could and should be melded with an increased and reindexed family allowance.
The NDP also has a long-standing policy to increase the refundable child tax credit by 80 per cent as an essential step toward lifting low-income families with children above the poverty line. If we have a commitment to children, if we have a commitment to families, then let us do it now, and not wait until after the election.
In the same vein, I heard my friend, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), suggesting that absolute necessities of life such as bread, milk, butter and a few similar products should not be subject to sales tax. I am not sure if he was trying to draw a distinction between all groceries and certain limited essentials. However, I want to serve notice on the Government again that it would perform a major disservice to Canadians, and would make a fundamental political error, if it ever again tried, as the Minister of Finance did a year ago in June, to impose a sales tax on the groceries Canadians buy every week. That is a fundamentally unacceptable position. We do not accept it. We fought it from the moment it was proposed. The Minister, after six months, finally backed off. However, on behalf of average Canadians, we say that this is

Income Tax and Related Acts
an unacceptable provision and we will not accept it. Do not let us see the Government going back on that promise.
I want to go on now to deal with the corporate side. It is significant that the increase in taxes on corporations under the Conservatives is far less proportionately than that which took place under tax reform in the U.S. In fact, I think there is a lot of deception taking place on this issue. The marginal rates on high income individuals in the U.S. are much higher than the Progressive Conservatives try to pretend. Corporate taxes went up far more there than in this country. It is interesting that the Conservatives, having promised in 1984 that a minimum tax would be brought in on individuals have failed to do so on corporations. Yet it has been estimated that a minimum tax on corporations of 20 per cent, which is the rate applied in Ronald Reagan's America, would bring in an extra $2 billion a year here in Canada. That would in turn allow tax cuts for average Canadians.
It is also notable that that would sharply cut down if not eliminate the large number of profitable Canadian corporations, some 60,000 or so, who will continue to be able to avoid tax on their profits after tax reform.
New Democrats suggest there should be a minimum tax on corporations here in Canada. If it can be brought in in corporate America despite Reaganomics, for goodness' sake, we can do it here in this slightly more progressive country. I suggest we should be doing that now. We should not be waiting. We should bring in the minimum tax. That is another way of assuring average Canadians that when they pay their fair share, everyone else is doing so as well.
I have had a great deal of correspondence from individual Canadians asking about the elimination of the $1,000 investment income tax deduction. The theory for removing it is quite strong in the sense that you make up for it by means of changes in the basic tax rates and credits and that kind of thing, and by not distinguishing between people who earn by working and those who earn from interest or dividend income. That I understand. However, the more I think about this, the more I realize that the reason people are really offended at that omission is the fact that the Government is cutting the taxes of wealthy Canadians, much of whose income comes from interest and dividends, and at the same time is taking away one of the few tax concessions given to average Canadians. That raises real questions in our minds.
I understand my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I would seek the indulgence of the House and ask for unanimous consent to continue, with the understanding that I would finish by one o'clock.

I suggest that in terms of simplicity we have a very serious problem. When I began to pay income tax 20 odd years ago my tax form was a dozen pages long, now it is 80 or 90 pages. I am overwhelmed with record keeping and the various ancillary documents I have to submit. Many other Canadians are suffering the same kind of thing. That is why New Democrats believe that there should be a plain language tax form. Why can the tax form for most Canadians not be a dozen pages or so, something we can fill in in the course of a couple of hours rather than having to consult a tax preparer and pay $50 or $200? The tax preparers often do not understand the law either. Why does it have to be so complicated? Why can it not be simple again? Why can we not provide people with a system which is both simple and fair?
Why can Revenue Canada officials not be available to meet with taxpayers on a regular basis to assist in tax filing? A constituent of mine who works here in the House of Commons told me the other day that for the last two weeks he has been trying to get the taxpayer inquiry number at the Revenue Canada office here in Ottawa. He has phoned morning, afternoon, and evening, day after day after day and that telephone number has been consistently busy. That, of course, is no service at all to the public. If he were Mr. White, working for the Prime Minister, or a colleague of Mr. Black, it would be available in black and white. He would have easy access to the people who could give him the tax information he needed. However, that is not available for average Canadians.
I want to turn now to the changes made by the Government since this first came forward in 1987. We know that the Government refused to move in a meaningful way in terms of the tax credit for children. It moved only with respect to the third and subsequent children. I grant that that was the Finance Committee's recommendation. I think the committee was wrong on that particular point. We argued very strongly against that. The Government increased the refundable tax credit by the magnificent sum of $35 per child but refused to raise the net family income threshold as the Finance Committee had proposed.
On automobile expenses the Government proposals are of a mind-boggling complexity. It refused to listen to the Finance Committee. I want to tell the Minister of State for Finance and his boss that every small business in the country is up in arms over that particular provision. They will be spending thousands of dollars every year just to try to administer this particular law in its proposed complexity. The 27-cent and 21cent feature which was added in the final run might alleviate things a bit. We will study that in the committee.
However, it does not have to be this complicated in order to prevent business people from driving a BMW or a Jaguar to work on the firm. That is what we want to eliminate. That is what offends average Canadians who are nursing an eight-year old car and do not understand how someone else can drive a very expensive automobile on the firm.

With respect to the taxation on farming, the Government has listened to a certain extent, and I say thank you for that. The Government's proposal for a modified accrual system of accounting on farms was going to offend and outrage every farmer across the country. It was not workable, it was not fair, and it was not reasonable. I am glad to see that the Government has finally backed away from that particular proposal and is now looking at this in more detail.
In other areas, however, the listening was a little less intense. I note, for example, that the Government refused to impose the alternative minimum margin tax which was unanimously proposed by the Finance Committee and would have had the effect of bringing in some $400 million a year from under-taxed sectors, that is, the banks and other financial institutions. In other words, the Government caved in to the lobby from the banks and other financial institutions. It came in with a temporary capital tax on the charter banks of one or one and a quarter per cent, which the Minister of State for Finance himself knows is a perpetuation of an archaic tax. If the Minister wants to move on the sales tax because it is archaic, why is the Government perpetuating an archaic tax?

The revenue that will come in is an estimated $120 million in the first year and $125 million in the second year. The committee proposed unanimously, with the support of the Conservative Members, a $400 million increase in revenues. That would have enabled us to create a fairer tax system, but the Government did not want to offend the banks by doing that.
It is interesting that the Government has moved a little bit on some technical provisions with respect to the "put in use" rule relative to the capital cost allowance but, having plugged a few loopholes, it now starts to open them again, most notably with the guarantee of a tax ruling on the Revenue Department with respect to the expenditures on the Hibernia project which it seems to me now sets a precedent for every other corporate interest to look for similar treatment. We will be back very quickly to where we were under the Liberals.
The Government did not accept the Finance Committee's recommendations of an advanced corporation tax or to close the preferred share dividend loopholes available to large corporations. There, too, I think the Finance Committee was well in advance of the Government. Again, the people who benefit the most from things like the preferred share dividend loophole or the moving of dividends from one company to another are Conrad Black and Peter White in the Prime Minister's Office. Only four or five days ago he was in Toronto fiddling around with preferred tax share dividends and that kind of thing in order that ordinary taxpayers would have to pay more so that he and his corporate associates could make more and more bucks.

Nonsense, we removed all that.

The Minister of State for Finance says "nonsense", yet it is true and he knows it. He used to teach business at Western Ontario and he should know that that kind of thing is going on.
The committee recommended that legitimate out-of-town travel expenses for sales purposes, et cetera, should not be subjected to the 80 per cent rule on entertainment and meal expenses. The Government did not grant that, and I think it was wrong. Instead, the Government has left the situation that legitimate business travel will only be deductible to 80 per cent, but if Labatt's from London wants to invest $200,000 in a VIP box at the Skydome it will be able to deduct 80 per cent of that cost as a business entertainment expense.
Again, there is some disparity in that. The small business here in Ottawa in the hightech industry which is trying to crack the European market will find that the cost of maintaining its representative in Europe for a week or two while on a sales trip is not fully deductible, but the expense for a box at the Skydome is 80 per cent deductible. There is something wrong with that.
The final point I wish to raise on that particular issue is that the Government has refused to move with respect to the recommendations coming from the tax fraternity on the issue of anti-avoidance. I would like to read an excerpt from the submission made by the Joint Committee of the Bar Association and the Association of Chartered Accountants. They said:
The Joint Committee is fundamentally opposed to the introduction of a general anti-avoidance rule of the kind included in the draft legislation of April 13, 1988. The Committee is unanimous in its view that the existing statutory rules (with relatively minor modifications) and jurisprudence are adequate to combat unacceptable tax avoidance.
The general anti-avoidance rule in the form proposed by the Minister of Finance is unnecessary, undesirable and represents a retrograde step in the evolution of Canada's income tax system. The introduction of such a rule will create an aura of uncertainty over ordinary business and commercial transactions for many years to come.
They strongly recommended two changes. The one which was accepted was to rule out Section 245(10). The one which was refused was to put the onus of proof onto the Minister of National Revenue.
I cited that because the committee itself felt that way too. It believed that if the Government had administratively been prepared to enforce the existing rules about anti-avoidance it would have been much more effective than bringing in new jurisprudence which will take seven or eight years to be clarified. In the meantime the Government is giving many firms a licence to cheat, firms which will not be caught under this new anti-avoidance rule.
The basic point which New Democrats have been making and will be making on the hustings is that New Democrats want a fairer tax system which benefits average Canadians. Tories want a Tory tax reform which benefits the wealthy and corporations. I believe that Canadians across the country want New Democratic tax reform and not Tory deform.
