Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Governments of Canada, Newfoundland and Labrador, and a consortium of oil companies announced the details of the largest development project ever undertaken in Atlantic Canada.
The project means thousands of quality jobs to Newfoundlanders and Atlantic Canadians. As the first major offshore development project in Canada, Hibernia will also generate significant new business opportunities for hundreds of companies in Newfoundland, Atlantic Canada, and other parts of Canada.
The project will take Canadian companies to the leading edge of offshore oil and gas development technology. Canadian companies can then plan an even larger role in future offshore projects both in Canada and around the world.
This project is great news for Newfoundland and Labrador, great news for Atlantic Canada, and great news for all of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers are faced with a drought this year that threatens their livelihood. The drought is also accelerating major changes in rural families. Women have always worked hard on the family farm, helping with the harvests, raising their children and maintaining the home. But now they are faced with another burden, seeking paid employment off the farm to pay the bills.
The number of farm women with outside jobs has increased dramatically over the last 30 years. In 1951, 13 per cent of farm women worked off the farm; in 1988, that number is 68 per cent.
Farm women face many obstacles in trying to combine their many responsibilities. There are inadequate child care facilities for their children in the rural areas where they live. The jobs available to most of these women are minimum wage employment. Farm women are still responsible for most of the housework and child care, and that in addition to helping with many tasks related to the farm. All of this makes for very long and demanding days.
I call upon the Government to offer concrete support to Canadian farm women, especially now because of the drought. More rural day care centres need to be established. Farm women's organizations need to be strengthened through increased funding. As well, women's contribution to the farm must be recognized through pension reform. Finally, farm women will benefit along with all Canadian women from effective employment equity legislation.

Mr. Speaker, when passing laws in this House sometimes our enthusiasm for a cause blinds us to the adverse effect and expense imposed on others. For example, we recently passed Bill C-204, the NonSmokers Health Act, which if proclaimed as is will impose severe constraints on VIA's operations. It will prevent VIA from offering smoking accommodation on more than 40 of its trains. In fact, Clause 5 will ban smokers entirely on all of its one-coach trains.
Also, VIA is discriminated against as it has no time limitations as provided for other modes, even though some trips last 75 hours. Additional equipment required to meet the requirements of the Bill will cost $8.5 million, and even worse, the rights of 300,000 smoking VIA passengers are negated and they will have to find other modes. Are smokers not Canadian citizens too?

subsubtopic: SUPREME COURT'S REFUSAL TO POSTPONE HEARING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning the Supreme Court of Canada summarily dismissed an application by the Government to postpone indefinitely the case of Borowski. In that particular case now pending before the Supreme Court, the court is being called to decide on the rights of the fetus.
The Government had the audacity to interfere in an unprecedented fashion in the process of the court. In effect, the Government asked the independent Supreme Court of this
July 19, 1988

country to dovetail its agenda into its own agenda, for political reasons.
Chief Justice Dickson of the Supreme Court of Canada was not persuaded. One could not help but be embarrassed for the lawyer from the Justice Department who was instructed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to argue a very weak case.
It was an abuse of the process. When will the Government have the courage to bring in legislation in order to protect the innocent unborn?
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in a letter dated February 24, 1984, when he was Leader of the Opposition, said:
On the overall issue of abortion, I realize that there are personal, moral and religious commitments on all sides of the abortion question, and I am not prepared to support abortion on demand.
I call on the Prime Minister to live up to his convictions and bring in legislation to protect human life right from the moment of conception.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pat Binns (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subsubtopic: CALL FOR SENATE TO PASS LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal dominated Senate is blocking progress in Atlantic Canada. It is holding up the Opportunities Agency legislation which is the best news for us since John Diefenbaker was Prime Minister.
We want to spend $1 billion in the next five years to let business develop their ideas, to create thousands of jobs and create long term prosperity.
Are the Senators, supported by Liberal Members of Parliament across the way, afraid we will get credit for new jobs and prosperity for Atlantic Canadians? Are they afraid of giving control to Atlantic Canada rather than keeping it here in Ottawa? Are they afraid we will succeed where they failed? Are they playing partisan politics on the backs of our small businessmen? This is an injustice to every Atlantic Canadian, to every Prince Edward Islander. We want jobs. We want prosperity.
I call upon the Liberal Members of Parliament to stand up, to get out of their seats, to walk over to the Senate right now and tell Mr. MacEachen and his colleagues that they are tired of being his patsies. Tell him he is wrong. Tell him you will support the Tories to develop Atlantic Canada.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF LONG-TERM DISASTER ASSISTANCE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, three years ago the Prairies experienced drought and grasshopper infestations. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) agreed then that ad hoc federal disaster assistance to Canadian farmers was inadequate. The Minister promised to do something about it. Three years have passed and we still have no sign of a long-term disaster assistance program.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, much of Canada is in the midst of the worst drought in over 50 years. The Government is providing some assistance to Canadian cattlemen. However, there is still no sign of help for Canadian grain farmers.
The uncertainty of government drought assistance is causing deep anxiety for tens of thousands of farm families. My colleagues and I join farm leaders across Canada who want to know what happened to the commitment of the Minister of Agriculture to create a permanent disaster assistance program. New Democrats call upon the Minister of Agriculture and the agricultural community to develop immediately a long-term assistance program, a program to cover crops, livestock and fixed assets, a long-term program that would greatly reduce the anxiety farm families face each time they are subjected to natural disasters.

Mr. Speaker, the Tour international de TAbitibi is the most important multi-stage junior cycling event in America. From July 26 to 31, 1988, a number of national teams including those of Switzerland, France, The Netherlands, Czechoslovakia, Guadeloupe and Canada will be on the starting line. A total of 25 teams will be taking part in the 20th edition of the Tour de I'Abitibi. The 20 years of dedicated work by people such as Leandre Normand, Marc Lemay, Robert Baril, Roland Lord, Andre Babin, Claude Page and thousands of volunteers have paid off. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: EXERCISE OF POLITICAL RIGHTS BY PUBLIC SERVANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the Federal Court of Appeal ruled on the political rights of federal public servants. The ruling invalidates section 32 of the Civil Service Employment Act, thereby granting the 214 000 public servants who come under this act the same political rights as all other citizens.
In so doing, the Court fulfilled the election promise which the Conservative Government was not able to keep. All interested parties expressed their satisfaction. Alliance President Daryl Bean called it a victory for all employees, one which allowed them to emerge from obscurity, and said that these new freedoms did not endanger the integrity of the Public service.
However, in its ruling the Court has created two categories of public servants. On the one side there are 214 000 public servants with full rights, and on the other there are 357 000 federal employees with no political rights.
I hope that the Government will have the courage to fulfill its 1984 promise and go all the way by granting full political rights to those Federal Government workers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
subsubtopic: CALL FOR SENATE TO PASS LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we heard Liberal Members in this House charge that the ACOA Bill will mean the end of the ID Division of Devco. Nothing could be more misleading. The ACOA Bill gives the ID Division the status of an independent Crown corporation. The ACOA Bill will give it a separate board of directors. If Liberal Members want an autonomous ID Division they should support Bill C-103. It is time to support Atlantic Canada, not the Godfather.
Cape Breton has never seen the growth of new industries and the commitment of federal money of the kind delivered since the election of this Government. Included are SI 10 million for Sysco modernization, tens of millions of dollars for Devco, more than $150 million for small business development, and more than $50 million under the tax credit program. Our record is clear. If the previous Liberal Government was as committed as we are, we would not be discussing unemployment in Cape Breton today.
Yesterday we learned about Hibernia. We will develop oil in the interests of Atlantic Canadians. The Liberals were determined to leave it under the sea.

Mr. Speaker, when rumours first circulated about the closure of the Newfoundland Railway, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) and Premier Brian Peckford of Newfoundland said that their first priority would be the workers who would lose their jobs. We learned on Sunday that the Minister for International Trade gave repeated assurances to the workers and the unions, saying to them behind closed doors: "Keep your mouths shut, and we'll look after you".
They were deceived. When the deal to close the railway was announced on June 20 there was nothing there from the Government of Canada for the 500 workers who would lose their jobs. They would get nothing that they were not already entitled to by their hard won collective agreements or existing employment contracts.
"Keep your mouths shut, and we'll look after you". Those are the words of the Minister for International Trade- patronizing workers, intimidation of possible opposition, and then a stab in the back. That is the arrogance of this Minister and this Government. That is how much they can be trusted.
When will the Government learn that people expect openness and honesty from government? The workers at the Newfoundland Railway got exactly the opposite.

subtopic: TOUR DE FRANCE-ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF CANADIAN CYCLIST
TOUR DE FRANCE-ACCOMPLISHMENTS OF CANADIAN CYCLIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the last two weeks Canadians have been following the heroic achievements of Steve Bauer, an Erie riding constituent who lives in Fenwick. He is in fourth place in the Tour de France, the world's most prestigious bicycle race.
To win this over 3,000 kilometre race which demands that riders pedal over mountain peaks from 4,000 to 7,000 feet in height, and speed across the borders of Belgium, Spain, Switzerland, and Italy, is considered to be cycling's highest honour. subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY LAY-OFFS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE URGED
ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY LAY-OFFS-GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the crisis on the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system continues. We still have in excess of 1,400 men and women, most of whom reside in the city of Thunder Bay and elsewhere along the system, who have been laid off. We have grain that is trickling to a slow stop coming from the west to a point at which we may only be handling 4 million tons for the next crop year.
I have raised this matter in the House. I have raised it directly with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) and with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. MacDougall) asking for some kind of program that will ensure that those people who are required to move Canada's gain through the eastern system are treated in the same way as those who are producing the grain, the farmers.
I call again on the Government to develop a program that will ensure that grain can move through the eastern system. Temporary elimination of Seaway tolls, lockage fees, and government imposed charges will help. The long term requires additional work.
We need to do what we can to protect those workers who are so vital to the system. I ask the Government to give consideration to changes to the unemployment insurance legislation so that those workers can be protected as well.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opposition fearmongers were wrong again. Last week, for days on end they tried to link the proposal to divert water from Lake Michigan to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Now the United States Army Corps of Engineers has decided not to go ahead with that diversion.
If water is part of the deal, why would the United States have done that? Could it be that water is not part of the deal? "'Tis so", cries the paranoid Opposition. One thing is certain, the Opposition intends to drag every red herring it can out of Canadian water.

Mr. Speaker, today is the ninth anniversary of the Nicaraguan people's victory over Samoza. A tiny country often invaded and ruled by the United States sacrificed many thousands of lives to rid the country of the last ruler left in place by the United States. Since then, the U.S. Government has tried to recover control of Nicaragua. It hired ex-National Guard officers with bloody records of brutality, and initiated a war of terrorism, concentrating on the killing of children, women, and unarmed campesinos.
[DOT] (U15)
Recently an uncertain ceasefire has been negotiated with the help of other Governments in Central America, South America, Europe and Canada. However, the U.S. has recently tried again to disrupt the peace through its ambassador, who openly encouraged a public demonstration which ended when the demonstrators attacked the police with stones and sticks and provoked the police response.
I call on the Government of Canada to follow the recommendation of the special committee and appoint a direct representative to Managua so that we no longer depend on the United States for our information about Nicaragua.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet decided that the region of Nagornno-Karabagh will remain part of Azerbaijan. This decision is a shock and huge disappointment to Armenians around the world. They had been hoping and praying that Karabagh would become part of Soviet Armenia. As I said in this House on March 1, 1988, the decision to separate this territory in 1923 was an injustice.
With Armenians accounting for at least 75 per cent of the population of Karabagh, they have everything in common with Soviet Armenia and nothing in common with the other citizens of Azerbaijan. In fact, they have suffered human rights violations and many have been killed.
This was one of the most important tests of General Secretary Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of glasnost. He has failed in his first major test. Canadians of Armenian heritage will not forget nor will they give up. The struggle for human dignity and justice will continue.

subtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF HIBERNIA OILFIELD-STATEMENT OF PRINCIPLES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. subtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF HIBERNIA OILFIELD-STATEMENT OF PRINCIPLES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF HIBERNIA OILFIELD-STATEMENT OF PRINCIPLES
speechtext: Land is indeed being bought and sold and scarce financial resources are being drawn to offshore related activities in the expectation of a guaranteed return. My question to the Deputy Prime Minister, and perhaps to the Hon. Member for St. John's West, is the following. I ask the Minister whether he is prepared to confirm today in the House that, notwithstanding the stated intentions contained in the Statement of Principles, what in fact was announced yesterday in St. John's was merely a Statement of Principles and not a firm and legally binding agreement to proceed with Hibernia development.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: DEVELOPMENT OF HIBERNIA OILFIELD-STATEMENT OF PRINCIPLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what was announced yesterday in St. John's was just as described, an agreed statement of principles between the Government of Newfoundland, the Government of Canada, and the five oil companies that make up the consortium that is developing Hibernia. It was a result of two years of negotiations from June, 1986, and finally concluded on July 9, 1988. As is the usual practice, the detailed legal agreements will be completed before the end of March.
Major expenditures on the project will start in 1989. There will be an investment of $8.5 billion, the greatest investment in any single project ever in the Atlantic region, and ever in Newfoundland. There will be 35,000 direct and indirect jobs created in Newfoundland, and of course across Canada many thousands of others.
The people who stopped the development from 1980 to 1984 and tried to crush the Province and the Government of Newfoundland are the very people now across the House trying to sabotage the deal with this type of silly question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only thing the Opposition is attempting to sabotage is falsehoods. What we are trying to save and define is the truth. I thank the Member for St. John's West who stood on his feet, unlike the exercise that took place in St. John's, Newfoundland yesterday. There was quite a difference, Mr. Speaker. Yesterday it was a firm deal, Tfoday the Minister has confirmed it is merely a Statement of Principles.
The first principle contained on page 1, paragraph 2 of the document, is the following:
The execution of this Statement of Principles by the signatories hereto is not
intended to and does not create legally enforceable rights or obligations
between the signatories hereto or between any of the signatories hereto and
any third parties ...
The Member for St. John's West, who is a Newfoundland Member of Parliament, shares with me and every Newfoundlander a desire for development, but also a desire not to see people's hopes crushed or their investments burned. Is he prepared to say clearly today, out of all the confusion, all of the hoop-la, and all the smoke and mirrors, that that article, that escape clause that precedes every other statement in yesterday's announcement, makes it possible for any one of the partners from now to March 31, 1989, to cancel out of this deal at any time without penalty? Is he prepared to confirm that?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will confirm this, Mr. Speaker, that five major oil companies have entered into a compact with the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland, the principles of which are set out in the agreement made public yesterday that will result in a $5.2 billion dollar capital expenditure off the coast of our province. It will put a firm
July 19, 1988

economic base under the economy of the Province of Newfoundland for the first time in 450 years. Every Newfoundlander, except those who are jealous or those who are politically motivated, is claiming that this is a great day.

You should know.

saying with respect to that deal, "We don't have the money" as is reported in today's Financial Post? What kind of Statement of Principles was announced yesterday? When will that Statement of Principles be kept as a firm, legal, binding document?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that Hibernia project is going. It is agreed. The companies have agreed. The Government of Canada has made it all possible with the initiative that we have taken and with the agreements that we have made. They will all be legally bound at the end of March. In the meantime, we are morally bound. We are completely bound. We are bound by our word. We are bound by the handshakes exchanged. And, Mr. Speaker, the proof of the pudding will be in the eating.
Those people who tried to crush the Government of Newfoundland, who stopped development for four years, who sat in their seats here and did nothing, the Benedict Arnolds, have failed, and their last minute attempts to sabotage this project will fail as well. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same Minister. He talked a lot about being bound. The fact is the one that is bound most is the Province of Newfoundland. speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):

Newfoundland, the gravity base structure is constructed in Newfoundland, 50 per cent of design engineering is done in Newfoundland, and 35,000 jobs will be had in Newfoundland. Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of thinking that resulted in the betrayal of Newfoundland from 1980 to 1984. When Mr. Peckford wanted to settle with Mr. Trudeau, what did Mr. Trudeau say to him? structure are going to be built. I would sooner be older and less wise than a puking babe, Mr. Speaker.

Fortune has turned for Newfoundland because of our Prime Minister and our Government, and Premier Peckford and his Government, not because of the saboteurs and people who never take a risk on the other side of this House!
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec has used the availability of low cost energy to attract industry for many years. Much of it is derived from the Churchill Falls hydro power. speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Communications) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-136, an Act respecting broadcasting and to amend certain Acts in relation thereto and in relation to radiocommunication, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be speaking in this debate this afternoon. I say that because what we are doing is moving steadily forward on a process which was begun some three years ago with the establishment of a task force to review the broadcasting system of this country, the Caplan-Sauvageau task force. There were then many weeks and months of detailed study by the parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, with the intervention of many individuals and organizations all across the country to bring to fruition a new Broadcasting Act for Canada.
When this broadcasting Bill received first reading just a few weeks ago, I stated at that time that it contained vital measures which would affect for many years what Canadians viewed on their television screens and listened to on their radios.
Broadcasting, without question, is the most pervasive cultural medium in the country. That is why I am convinced that Bill C-136, the new Broadcasting Act, is far more than just a set of business criteria governing an industry. It goes to the very heart of our culture and of our country.

I am pleased to have an opportunity to tell my colleagues in the House how important this Bill is. I will be telling them why I think it ought to be passed quickly.
July 19, 1988



Clause 3 of the Bill is, of course, the key article and is fundamental to understanding the thrust of Bill C-136. It is a statement of principles. It states clearly that radio frequencies are public property and that broadcasting is a public service "essential to the maintenance and enhancement of national identity and cultural sovereignty", irrespective of the method of transmission. The broadcasting system, as stated in Clause 3, should serve to "safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada". These statements, and the redefinitions of broadcasting terms, represent a recasting of the regulatory landscape to reflect the dynamics of modern Canadian society.
The influence of broadcasting is known to all Members. The power of radio and television to inform, to sell, to mold opinions, to create personalities, to provide people from coast to coast with a shared experience is enormous. It is unparalleled.
While this Bill seeks to carry the broadcasting industry into the 21st century, it also recognizes the central role that it plays in the lives of most Canadians. For example, in just one week a typical Canadian listens to between 18 hours and 24 hours of radio and 24 hours of television. It is therefore fundamentally important to our political and our cultural sovereignty that our broadcasting system be an accurate reflection of who we as Canadians are, how we behave and how we view the world.
In addition to these social considerations, there are other external pressures threatening the broadcasting system, pressures endangering the ability of our broadcasters to remain competitive and to explore new ways of contributing to the choices of programming that are available and must be available to all Canadians.
As you know, Sir, the existing Broadcasting Act was passed in 1968-20 years ago. It is based on one technology, the technology of over-the-air broadcasting transmitters. New technologies, ones which do not use this spectrum, are increasingly making obsolete current definitions of what constitutes broadcasting as written into the 1968 Act. New technologies have emerged which are not included or defined in that piece of legislation and are therefore making that Act increasingly obsolete.
Existing technologies, ones which have come into being in more recent years such as cable and satellite dishes, do not fit easily into the 1968 Act. We have had to turn to the courts again and again to determine whether they fall within the jurisdiction of existing broadcasting legislation.

The courts confirmed that the 1968 legislation applied in certain cases but not in others. Every time the scope of these definitions gets narrower the Government loses some of its
Broadcasting Act
ability to set the socio-cultural aims of broadcasting on behalf of all Canadians.

We face the challenge of drafting legislation that can deal with the technology of today, as well as the technology of tomorrow. Our solution is not to add to existing definitions; it is to allow broadcasting technology to evolve by freeing it of legislation that defines the medium of technology.
The approach of Bill C-136 is to be technology-neutral. Broadcasting is defined by content, not by the way it is received by the audience. The signal is not the key. What the signal carries is the important factor.
This technology-neutral approach means that distribution systems can use the technology of their choice. It also ensures that Bill C-136 will keep its legal foundation in the face of future technological development, something which is very critical if the institutions that govern the broadcasting system are not to have their power eroded.
There are increasing societal pressures which demand attention as well. Since 1968 our society has evolved and has changed in many areas. For instance, there is now the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the changing role of women, Meech Lake, the recognition of distinct French and English-speaking societies, the growing awareness of our multicultural diversity, the recognition of aboriginal claims and rights-all these developments are changing how we approach broadcasting and what is expected of the medium. The pressure for legislation which recognizes this evolving reality is growing upon us every day.

The particular context of English and French broadcasting commands our attention as well.
The presence of two official languages is more than a simple constitutional reality, it is a fact throughout our broadcasting networks. Bill C-136 explicitly acknowledges the existence of our two official languages as well as the fact that the economic and cultural reality is not the same for English and French broadcasters, that their requirements may differ.
The Bill stipulates that the programming provided by the CBC should reflect the different needs and circumstances of each official language community, including the particular needs of English and French linguistic minorities.
The CRTC must apply these regulations with flexibility and take into account the different characteristics of English and French broadcasting. For instance the Bill has a clause concerning the establishment of a wide array of English and French broadcasting services throughout the country. With this clause the CRTC will be in a position to require that more French services be made available to francophones outside Quebec, in addition to those provided by Radio-Canada. This clause also shows that the Government is committed to expand services intended for official language minorities.

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act

With the rapid progress in broadcast technology Canadians are demanding an ever greater variety of choice. Our broadcasting system provides a truly remarkable range of radio and television signals. There are literally hundreds of radio signals in the country. Cable television carries dozens of channels. The mix includes private and public stations, both in English and in French, as well as Canadian and foreign programming.
However, in their demands for more and better choice, Canadians are sending a message that is loud and clear. It is: "We want access to increased Canadian choice especially in prime time." That is the message. That was the message that I took to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in February of 1987 when it began studying the Caplan-Sauvageau report.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Government had just received the report of the task force on broadcasting policy, a report which has been referred to many times in this Chamber and elsewhere. This report was referred to the standing committee for examination and for recommendations. The committee studied it in detail over a period of months-indeed, for one year and a half. I said at the time that I first addressed the committee on this subject that I was convinced that the Canadian broadcasting system is the nervous system of our country. It links us together. I told the standing committee at that time that, more than ever, "broadcasting must be seen as a fundamental part of cultural policy."
It was clear then, and it remains clear today, that any initiative must set out the over-all broadcast framework policy, the broad policy under which we must operate, outlining the objectives of the broadcasting system as a whole, as well as the mandate, structure, and powers of both the CRTC and of the CBC.
As I told the standing committee at that time, our ultimate concern must be with the content of programming that is and must be available to Canadians. We must address both the quantity of Canadian programming and its quality if we are to promote viewing acceptance by the public. If we are to have the audiences that we think are vital to Canadian programming we must be sure of the quality of that programming as well as its quantity.
A nation's fictional repertoire is the life-blood of its culture. We must never underestimate the impact of dramatic television programming for, within it, I would say we find the surest expression of our cultural values, of the way we live, as well as our collective memory.
We do indeed share the life experiences of people in other countries. But, as Canadians, we experience them in our own way. We must ensure that we have the opportunity to share this experience with each other, and to appreciate the heritage we enjoy as Canadians-and we must do it, Mr. Speaker, in prime time.
Bill C-136 promotes this imperative. It will strengthen Canadian programming; it will enrich our culture and our national identity; it will permit us to embrace new technologies; it will provide the choices that Canadians expect and want; and it will strengthen Canadian broadcasting.
I would like to make it very clear that this Bill does not seek to limit choice and does not restrict choices. But to ensure that competitive Canadian programming is a central component of an even greater choice of viewing and listening options, the Canadian choices must be there. This means additional Canadian drama and variety must be seen and must be shown in prime-time English television, and also improvements in the production quality of French-language television.
I want to make it very clear that this legislation does not erect barriers against programming that is not Canadian. Canadians now, for the most part, are able to access programming directly from a variety of sources in the United States. What we are talking about here is the encouragement of the production of more Canadian programming by a broadly based approach involving all the players in the broadcasting system. I want to talk about those various players for a brief time, because so often in the past we have considered the players being solely the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We must go beyond that.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is vital in this enterprise. Bill C-136 makes clear the central role of the CBC and, in particular, its responsibility for the provision of Canadian programming. The CBC will serve Canadians by providing a distinctly Canadian viewpoint in its programming, including news, variety, drama, and sports.
The Government believes very strongly that Canadians deserve genuinely Canadian popular choice programming which may be different in emphasis from the offerings that private commercial stations give us. We are giving the CBC the financial means of creating programming aimed at the interests of the Canadian audience. We are increasing the CBC's budget by $35 million a year above and beyond its annual increase for inflation. That $35 million is money that is directed to programming. Of that $35 million, $20 million is targeted to help the CBC meet its goal of 95 per cent Canadian content on prime-time English television. The other $15 million is intended to help Radio-Canada increase the production budgets for French language programs. The CBC will remain what it has always been: the principal vehicle for cultural expression in Canada.
We are also strengthening the accountability of the CBC, as recommended by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. At the same time, we are guaranteeing the CBC's independence in programming and operations. I want to underline, Mr. Speaker, that the corporation's freedom of expression and its journalistic, artistic, and programming independence is safeguarded for the first time in Bill C-136; it is written into the legislation.
July 19, 1988

The mandate of the CBC, as contained in this Bill, will mean that the CBC will lead in providing authentically Canadian choices, particularly in popular drama in both official languages. But the programming responsibility is net the CBC's alone. I mentioned the role of all of the players in the broadcasting system, and so I want to make it clear that the responsibility for Canadian programming does not rest solely with the CBC. For the first time private broadcasters have a specified legislated responsibility to contribute as well. The Bill contains a number of new instruments for the regulatory authority so that it will be better equipped to supervise the broadcasting system without excessively intrusive procedures. The new powers that are accorded to the CRTC will make this possible.
It is important to understand that broadcasters do not have the option of not doing, or doing less Canadian programming. That option does not exist for them. They cannot say that they will not do more, or they will do less. That is not an option. We are putting before them the means by which they too as private broadcasters can increase their Canadian content.
This Bill is a new approach. It gives the CRTC the tools to work more closely with private broadcasters so as to increase Canadian programming in vital but under-achieved target areas such as drama. The legislation includes the basis for a performance incentive which encourages individual broadcasters to increase the amount of specifically targeted areas of programming, notably drama, in a way which best responds to their economic capabilities. That is above and beyond the Canadian content that is now expected of them.
We will ask the CRTC to hold hearings on applying the performance incentives and to recommend the best use of the incentives. This innovative new tool will give English language broadcasters in particular an added incentive to invest in quality Canadian programming. It is worth noting that private broadcasters themselves say that quality Canadian programming makes good sense. It distinguishes them from the competition. Canadians have said time and again that they will watch quality Canadian programming. Canadians have shown it. I would say to you that French-speaking Canadians have done so and shown so for decades,
Bill C-136 also provides an Alternative Programming Service to meet needs not fulfilled by existing mass entertainment broadcasters. This service has been discussed in many ways: by the task force, by the parliamentary committee and by advisers to my Department from the industry. This service will provide the kind of programming that does not appear, or only rarely appears, on existing television outlets. A key role of the Alternative Programming Service will be the portrayal of Canada's multicultural nature to Canadians as a whole.
Canada, as you know, does not have a uniform single culture but a diversity of cultures. The Alternative Programming Service mandate will provide all Canadians with a more
Broadcasting Act
realistic view of the multicultural realities in all parts of the country, and that is so critically important as the diversity of our country becomes greater and as the strengths and the benefits that that diversity provides become better known. This new service's innovative programming will complement large audience programming, and it will cater to tastes and to interests hot provided for by mass producers. The process of establishing the Alternative Programming Service should be completed within two years.
Programs from across the country, regional programs, programs through the multicultural dimension, programs of the performing arts, all these will be part of the new service's specific mandate which is anchored in Bill C-136.
This Bill also recognizes the unique contribution which distribution services are making. While cable is the most common method of distribution, others are emerging. I refer specifically to subscription television, satellite master antenna television, multi-channel, multi-point distribution systems, and satellite direct-to-home, to name but a few of the new distribution systems that now exist.

Bill C-136 acknowledges that cable TV has expanded considerably since the Broadcasting Act became law in 1968, reaching into more than 70 per cent of Canadian households and altering the basic concept of broadcasting.
Time has come to define anew the role of cable TV operators. Are they just like ordinary companies, or should they be expected to play a wider role and shoulder heavier responsibilities in the field of broadcasting?
As it happens, cable TV companies are already actively involved in programming, particularly with respect to French broadcasting.
The Bill acknowledges the fact and provides that program producing distributors open access to non-affiliated services.

The CRTC is being given the power to mediate disputes between broadcasters and cable distributors. The distributors involved in programming will still be subject to CRTC approval and Control, and they will be required to meet the objectives of the broadcasting policy. That is written into Bill C-136. All distributors, whether involved in programming or not, will be required to continue to give Canadian programming a priority.
I would like to comment briefly as well on the way in which this legislation deals with the questions of fairness and access. The past two decades have been marked by a growing awareness of human rights. Canada has repatriated the Constitution and has entrenched within it a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The accessibility of broadcast media to all Canadians, the way in which broadcasting reflects Canadians to themselves,

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act
and the fairness with which it handles different points of view, these are all addressed in this Bill.
This legislation also recognizes the needs of Canadians living outside of urban areas, recognizes the needs of aboriginal peoples, and the special needs of Canadians with physical disabilities.
Hear, hear!

The Government has already announced a number of initiatives to bring distribution systems to small communities, communities that are more remote, and as well has undertaken to provide a satellite distribution system for the reading service of the blind.
I return to the need to stop the erosion of the institutions to regulate and direct the broadcasting system, because that is what has been happening in recent years.
Bill C-136 therefore does not base its definition of broadcasting in technology, but takes a technology-neutral approach.
The major participants in broadcasting can therefore expand and change with the most effective, the most profitable, technologies that they can utilize. Bill C-136 opens the door. It does not limit technologies in the way in which they can be employed, in delivering broadcasting services across the country.
Because it is not solely rooted in technology, the federal Government's ability to exercise its jurisdiction will again be firmly established and will not be challenged as technologies continue to change.
In summary, let me recapitulate why Bill C-136 is vital for this country. It establishes primacy for Canadian programming. It reflects the linguistic duality and the differences in English and in French broadcasting. It ensures that Canadian culture, Canadian tastes and society are reflected in programming and in operations. It provides all Canadians with access to a wide range of radio and television signals. It is technology-neutral and able to accommodate technological changes. It provides for an efficient and responsive CBC and CRTC.

With this Bill the Governement wants to promote our national culture and identity.

I want to say that I am very proud of this Bill. It has come about as the result of the work of a large number of people. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Cabinet, the members of the standing committee who worked for so many months, the Caplan-Sauvageau task force and all its members, the many Canadians who have appeared to express their views, individually and collectively, as organizations, have all had a major input into this piece of legislation.
I may say that no piece of legislation will ever satisfy everyone, in all of its details, but I am pleased with the initial response-whether it is from people in the media or organizations or groups across the country-to the way in which we are moving on this Bill. I am sure that it has been a collective effort and one in which I think the House can take a lot of pride. The Bill itself, I believe, will ensure the existence of a vibrant and dynamic Canadian broadcasting industry well into the 21st century. It will as well foster a cultural identity that is distinctively and uniquely Canadian. I am sure that that is what we all are seeking to attain.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Could I get unanimous consent to ask the Minister a question?
That is fine with me.

Agreed.
