speechtext: As unanimous consent has not been granted, we will resume debate. The Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).
I have the sense that the Minister was prepared to answer, Mr. Speaker.
Yes.

I am quite pleased to rise to speak to this Bill. I acknowledge to the Minister that this has been a tour de force. There have been inputs from large sectors of Canadian society to the Bill itself. These people have not as yet had the opportunity to examine the actual Bill which, as I am sure the Minister will agree, was only tabled a couple of weeks ago.
The Minister should receive a medal for the star performance which I accord her for getting this Bill through Cabinet and for getting permission to have it on the docket at this fast rate. In that regard I think we are all quite pleased to see this Bill coming to the point of its natural rotation of every 20 years so we can have a new look at what is happening in this incredibly swiftly evolving and changing telecommunications world in which we live.
That being said, it meets the commitment of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who during his campaign in August, 1984, undertook to see to a new communications legislation which the Minister is now bringing forward in the summer of 1988. I find the timing rather interesting and I would like to comment on that for a moment.
It is prime-time.

It is prime-time? I wonder whether it is prime-time, Mr. Speaker. This is the summer which is a time
July 19, 1988

when people are out relaxing, not paying much attention to the public agenda. It is interesting to note that the public agenda of those matters, which I believe fundamentally touch the character, the nature and the kind of people we are as Canadians, has been addressed during the summer months. We came back here two summers ago for a criminal issue. Last summer we came back because we were being inundated with refugees and we had to address a new immigration Bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Thanks to the Senate we are still here.
We addressed as well at that time the Meech Lake Bill. This summer we are dealing with free trade and now broadcasting.
All this and more.

If you look at the implication of what Canada is, who composes Canada, which the immigration and refugee Bills do, and if you talk about Meech Lake and the organization of this country, if you look at free trade and its potential impact on the future organization of this land, and then look at the broadcasting Bill, which as I think the Minister mentioned and which I would like to underscore, is one of the most powerful mediums of communication, education, information that impacts on society, you will note that here we are addressing this issue in the middle of the holiday season when there is very little interest about how we share and communicate with one another. I find this a little sad because we are talking about local, national and international future impacts.
This powerful medium, TV, radio and cinema form that part of our lives, and when you think about it, watching television is the number one leisure activity for Canadians. Canadians spend more than 24 hours each week on average in front of a television set. Each year Canadian children watch almost 1,000 hours of television compared to the 800 hours they spend in school. It is little wonder that they have an interesting perspective on what is Canada and how they will perceive things as they grow into adulthood and hopefully become interested in active political life. How will their thinking evolve with the impact of our public media on their lives and thought processes? Ninety-five percent of Canadians are radio listeners, spending 18 days a week on that activity. Two-thirds of Canadians say watching television is their favourite pastime, and more than 50 per cent of Canadians say that broadcasting is still their principal source of news and information.
1 suggest that this Bill, which the Minister, with a degree of pride that is well earned, brings forward today, is one that will have a fundamentally important impact on the sovereignty of this country. That is why it is of great concern to me.
The standing committee tried very hard to remain nonpartisan and non-politicized, although we had one unfortunate fall out over All-News. That aside, I think in general we have
Broadcasting Act
been of one mind with respect to how we should perceive this very important industry. We have all said that there is nothing wrong with having access to the wider world, notwithstanding the fact that there is an inordinate amount of American programming on our television screens. It is also very critical that Canadians have access to programs and movies, entertainment, information and enlightenment which represent our own cultural values. That is what we are missing. There are so many more hours of American news available which I think could have a very serious impact on us.
In order to remain as non-partisan as possible in this undertaking, I would like to put on record what some of the groups who have been looking at this Bill have to say. I am sure the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) will listen and address these issues and concerns in the legislative committee, but which will be addressed to our standing committee sometime, I hope in the very distant future, but anyway-
Don't say that.

What has been said in Le Devoir? [Translation]
... in the Saturday July 16, 1988 edition of Le Devoir. The author of this article, Mrs. Esther Desilets, is Director General of the Canadian Institute of Adult Education. What happens to the CBC's mandate? That's the question she asks. And she adds:
The long-awaited Broadcasting Bill is the culmination of an extensive process of reflection and consultation which the Canadian Institute of Adult Education has followed closely.
There is reason to be happy, of course, that the Bill recognizes major achievements such as the leading role of the CBC and the public nature of the broadcasting system as a whole. However, the CIAE considers that the Bill has major faults which must be corrected if the present situation is to improve.

These are the observations where they find some errors or holes in the legislation which they feel need to be addressed.

The first is:
Political Control over the CRTC
The Bill proposes major changes concerning the CRTC. While reaffirming the need to put a single independant public agency in charge of regulating and monitoring the system, it does not increase its powers. It increases rather the powers of the Government and the Minister.
The Bill would enable the Government to issue directions concerning all the CRTC's activities except the granting and renewing of broadcasting licenses. As far as broadcasting licenses are concerned, however, the Government would be able to send back and reverse CRTC decisions. Furthermore, the Government could exempt broadcasters from certain provisions of the Bill.
Under the Free Trade Agreement, the Governor in Council will also have the power to issue directions to the CRTC as to the implementation and interpretation of the clause dealing with copyrights and integral rebroadcasting of American signals.

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act
Finally, upon request from the Government, the CRTC could require that stations broadcast programs which the same Government feels are urgent in nature and of great significance for the Canadian people. We can foresee already the possible risk of frequencies being used for political partisanship.
The legislation does not provide for any real public consultation mechanisms concerning these directions. The policies and regulations developed by the CRTC have always been scrutinized during public hearings. Well, government orders provide only for very limited consultation mechanisms.
While supporting the principale that our elected representatives and the Government are responsible for developing major broadcasting guidelines, we cannot agree with the proposed political control measures on the broadcasting system. This control is much more political than democratic in nature.
Private broadcasters.
It should be recognized, however, that some recommendations in the Bill will reinforce the power of the CRTC over private corporations. Private corporations will have to respect more CRTC's regulations and decisions, as a result of to the explicit power given to the commission to issue licensees with binding orders. The Commission will also be empowered to levy a performance fee for broadcasting certain types of Canadian programs. It is to be hoped that these new measures will prove efficient.
Finally we note that the real monitoring power of the CRTC will not be reinforced by an extension from five to seven years of the licence renewal period. In this area, we would prefer, as suggested by the CPCC, that the CRTC should issue more frequently license renewals of less than five-year duration.
A Canadian Broadcasting Corporation with a different vocation? The vital importance of the CBC is clearly reaffirmed in this Bill. Moreover, this recognition is reinforced by supplementary budgets. That is the most interesting aspect of the new policy.
We wonder however about the proposals which might alter the CBC's vocation. When we compare the clauses in this Bill with those in the 1968 legislation, we realize that such a possibility exists.
According to the current legislation, the CBC should be "a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of programming in fair proportion".
According to Clause, 3(1 ){m) of this Bill, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as the national broadcaster, should provide radio and television services incorporating a wide range of information and entertainment programming that is predominantly and distinctly Canadian.
What will happen to the CBC's mandate concerning the broadcasting of programs for people of different ages, sexes, cultures and tastes? It is stated further that in the evening, during prime time, CBC will offer Canadian programs which are likely to appeal to the widest audience and that such an effort is necessary to justify the subsidies granted by Parliament and obtain the advertising money it needs.
There is the mass audience appeal as opposed to the "large" appeal that CBC had before.

There is ample reference to TV dramas, as if that was the essential part of TV programming. What about news, public affairs, cultural programs? Is the CBC recognized a specific role in those areas?
A reading of the proposals suggests that the only aspect that would set CBC's programming apart from private sector programming would be the quantity of Canadian productions as compared to American productions.
It goes on to say:
In the area of news and programs to satisfy more diversified tastes and smaller audiences, they proposed alternative programming. Although in the legislation there is reference to alternative services in French and in English, in fact one English language service only is in play, the French speaking public having to be content with TV 5 and existing services.
What is the next question?
French language television.
The recognition of the specific nature of French-language TV is a welcome fact. But what is behind that principle? On closer look, the proposals would rather seem to increase the imbalance between services offered in French and in English. Although new English services are proposed, when it comes to French services the only proposal is for improvements to existing ones.
The policy declaration is based on the fact that French-speaking audiences already are getting from Radio-Canada and Radio-Quebec a programming that meets its tastes and special interests, and that soon TV 5 will be added to those services, while such needs are not covered on the English side, whence the proposal for an English-language alternative service.
It may not be warranted to multiply French language programming services because of the limited size of the French-speaking market. However, there should be an attempt at assessing the impact on the development of Frenchspeaking culture of the lack of new programming services in such strategic areas as news and culture.
Currently, the specific needs for specialized broadcasts of a major part of the French-speaking population are no more covered than those of the Englishspeaking public. Radio-Quebec, in the evening, increasingly tends to target the larger audience. TV 5's future programming will not either meet the requirements for alternative programmings services proposed in the legislation.
Measures to improve the quality of French-speaking programming will not have such a significant impact as is being implied. Of course, a $15 million budget increase over the next two years is an improvement. But, in view of the current imbalance-in the order of 50 per cent-between French and English-language production budgets, this measure seems to provide for a catching up rather than for real development.
In order to increase Canadian programming, the statement suggests incentive bonuses. These bonuses will have practically no impact on the French programs produced by the private sector . ..
. . . and I can even add on the English programs as well.
The performance incentives will be determined by the number of drama and variety shows produced by private broadcasters. But, since the French private broadcasters already transmit more than five hours of drama shows a week, which is more than the suggested minimum, they will not benefit from this incentive.
Only the additional credits granted to Telefilm Canada for French productions will in fact benefit the French language television community. It's clearly insufficient. Democracy not at stake
July 19, 1988

And then, she adds:
This Bill is leaving unresolved some major problems related to the whole issue surrounding the control and the democratic access to the broadcasting system. As far as broadcast time for regional communities, various social groups and women organisations is concerned, the Bill suggests no real measures. It also avoids talking about the concentration of media ownership, offering no solution to the problem relating to the joint onwership of distribution and programming undertakings. Also, no specific recommendations apply to community broadcasting.
This Bill respecting broadcasting, as presented, is unacceptable. Some serious deficiencies will have to be corrected if we are to improve the broadcasting system and allow it to develop in conformity with the relevant social and cultural objectives. The Government has to provide for the creation of a parliamentary committee to study this Bill.

I think that is one of the best summaries of the concerns. I recall raising many of those concerns at the press conference following the deposition of the Bill by the Minister.
What does the Liberal Party think about the Bill?

I said at the very outset what the Liberal Party thinks about the Bill. I suggest that my hon. colleague not worry; he will hear in parliamentary committee what we think about this Bill. I have already made my point of view known.
The Canadian Conference of the Arts has some concern about cabinet power of direction. Paul Siren, President of the CCA, expressed some unease with regard to the Cabinet's seemingly unlimited power of direction over the CRTC while maintaining the Government's power to set aside or refer decisions back to the commission. He said that either of these measures would have been sufficient safeguards but that both would give the Government undue control over the arm's length regulator.
We in the committee did not necessarily agree with that point of view, but I would advise the Minister that there are important and substantive groups which see problems other than those the committee indicated.
With respect to alternative programming, the Canadian Conference of the Arts was also disappointed with the estimated two-year delay in the setting up of an alternative programming service. Other concerns include the provisions to allow cable operators to become programmers and broadcasters. The lack of consideration for regional production and programming needs is underscored as well as the state of the CBC all-news channel. These are serious concerns which they intend to bring to our attention in the parliamentary committee.
With regard to the CBC, ACTRA said:
The extra money that will be phased in hardly makes up for the millions the CBC has lost in cut-backs. And while the CBC is expected to fulfil a wide mandate, the money to go forward just isn't there. In short, this part of the
Broadcasting Act
announcement doesn't exactly make my socks roll up and down. The CBC's parliamentary appropriation for 1988-89 is $119.6 million less than the appropriation for 1984-85 in constant dollar terms.
With respect to alternative programming, ACTRA said:
It deserves scrutiny, because unfortunately it may contain some pitfalls. The notion that Canada needs another outlet for Canadian production, particularly of the kind that has no current access to the broadcasting system, is a good one. But, if the mandate of the service is too narrow, and the funding insufficient, it risks becoming a ghettoized service ignored by the viewers. If implemented to genuinely serve Canadians equally, it may prove a success.
With respect to cable companies, ACTRA said:
Cable should not be in production because there are too many possibilities for unfair corporate concentration. We've maintained that separating programmers from cable distributors provides for a much healthier climate. It's a shame the Government doesn't see it that way.
With respect to the Minister's discussion about the Canadian Charter and equality opportunities for both women and minorities, allow me to bring to the Minister's attention that Media Watch has been following this new Broadcasting Act and is concerned about serious omissions.
The Standing Committee on Communications and Culture supported a number of the Media Watch representations. It was convinced that special employment equity measures were necessary. The standing committee recommended that the Broadcasting Act include provisions designed to increase significantly the number of women and minority groups at all levels within broadcasting until equitable representation is achieved.
In this new Act, the purpose for which operations and therefore employment may be scrutinize^ is obscured. The Government claims that it is recognizing human rights in provision 3(1 )(c)(iii), but it chose not to define in clear terms that operations and programming come under scrutiny for the purpose of determining whether principles of equality are reflected. The CRTC authority to make real change in terms of employment equity is undermined in this new legislation and women are once again faced with legal and administrative battles which they can ill afford. I would suggest that the same holds true for minority groups. I regret that the CRTC was not given a direct and specific mandate to apply employment equity as part of its responsibility.
We have heard from other groups, and 1 wish to cite a very interesting observation which was brought to our attention this morning as we were involved with the free trade agreement. It comes from the Stratford Festival Company and is signed by nearly 350 employees at all levels including actors, producers, seamstresses, tailors, cutters, et cetera. They are concerned about the free trade agreement and the specific cultural provision in Article 2005 which exemplifies the kind of sell-out of our national sovereignty which they believe to be taking place. They are particularly concerned about the notwithstanding provision of the agreement. The example they use relates

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act
to broadcasting. I hope the Minister will have an adequate answer for this example. They say:
If a future government were to introduce a broadcasting Bill that specified
greater Canadian content-
I know that is what the Minister wants and that is why she has put incentives into the Bill. They continue:
-U.S. commercial interests could claim loss of revenue (less "Dallas" "Cosby Show" etc. on Canadian TV channels). The U.S. government could assess that loss as $X millions and take "measures of equivalent commercial effect" in, let's say, the Atlantic fisheries. Our Atlantic fishermen would naturally be outraged by the cultural initiative. Canadian would be set against Canadian and of course the new broadcasting Bill would be dropped. U.S. corporate interests would prevail.
They elaborate on this perspective with respect to how measures of equivalent commercial effect can open the door to American corporate intervention and interest. I suggest that these are serious concerns which ought to be addressed.
In terms of aboriginal languages the committee recommended that the new Act recognize the right of Canada's aboriginal peoples to receive service in representative native language where numbers warrant and as public funds become available. We went through a whole presentation on this issue, but in the final analysis the legislation does not assure service in representative native languages. I will save the Minister from all the details of this matter, but I will certainly bring it forward in committee. The Government has failed to act upon the committee's recommendation that the CBC offer services in the aboriginal languages. The National Aboriginal Communications Society has expressed its dismay about the failure of the Government to act on the committee's recommendation.
This legislation does not set limits on foreign broadcasting services in Canada. Recommendation No. 58 was that the Act should be drafted to define the essential role of distribution undertakings, those being cable, as that of distributing Canadian radio and television services in English and in French, both public and private, with first priority given to public sector Canadian services, followed by private Canadian services with the exception of the "three plus one" services already carried.
The Bill should make provision for the carriage of foreign radio and television services only when the programming they provide is complementary to that available from licensed Canadian broadcasters and network operators. The Bill should also provide for priority to be given to the carriage of services in French in distribution undertakings that serve primarily Francophone subscribers.
I see nothing in the Bill that will enforce the provisions found in Recommendation No. 58. In fact, there is great disappointment about tiering and the amount of carriage of non-Canadian services that will be allowed on extended basic cable according to the Government's Bill. The Minister will recall that our standing committee recommended limits on
those foreign broadcasting services in Canada. The Government claimed that this would unduly restrict the access of Canadians to a range of international broadcasting services and that its purpose was simply to encourage more high quality Canadian shows.
I suggest The Toronto Star sums up that response in a very significant and succinct way when it said: "Do statements like that mean Ottawa has declawed its broadcast policies in the same way it weakened its film distribution Bill to overcome American objections?" Did Jack Valenti write the script for this performance as well?
Let us consider vertical integration of distribution undertakings. The committee stated the following in Recommendation No. 51:
The Act should provide that no distribution undertaking may have an ownership interest in, or be in common ownership with, a pay television, specialty or any other network programming service distributed on such undertaking on the basis of a contractual relationship between the licensed network and the distribution undertaking, or where the consent of the network or the distribution undertaking is required for carriage.
There was very serious and long debate about this area and how it should be addressed. The Government decided on inaction on vertical integration. It chose not to preclude distribution undertakings from participating in programming and from participating as broadcasters. The Minister has rejected our recommendation, our recommendation in the committee's sixth report, in its policy report, and the recommendation in the Caplan-Sauvageau report that they not be allowed to be programmers and vice versa. There is an inherent conflict of interest. I hope the Minister will be open minded in addressing this issue in the committee.
I have had much comment on the legislation that weakens the CBC's regional programming role and lacks definition of the community sector. We have made it quite clear that the broadcasting industry should address the private, the public and the community sector. I know the Minister responds by saying it is covered under local broadcasting, but it is not defined who is responsible or how the community sector will be financed and by whom.
Our Recommendations Nos. 22 and 23 suggest that the Canadian broadcasting system should play an active role in stimulating a Canadian consciousness and should serve the special needs of each geographic region in both official language groups by contributing actively to the exchange of information and expression among the regions and between French and English speaking Canadians. The system should acquaint all Canadians with the traditions, values, practices, and aspirations of each region of Canada. I have said that there should be a footprint in both French and English right across this land as part of the fundamental characteristics of this land.
Recommendation No. 23 was that the Canadian broadcasting system should encourage the development of Canadian expression, providing a wide range of programming that
July 19, 1988

reflects Canadian attitudes, opinions, ideas, values, and artistic creativity; displaying Canadian talent in entertainment programming; and offering information and analysis concerning Canada and other countries from a Canadian point of view.
I suggest to the Minister that by changing the mandate and description of the responsibility of the CBC that particular responsibility has essentially been emasculated. The legislation states: "It is hereby declared as the broadcasting policy for Canada that the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should be varied and comprehensive, providing a balance of information, enlightenment and entertainment". The Government has removed "enlightenment" from the CBC's mandate, which is a serious responsibility. The Bill states that the system should reflect the regions rather than that each region should have a role.
As a result of the Government's cuts, CBC's service to the regions has been reduced by 28 per cent. Even the increase of $35 million a year to the CBC will do little to those Tory cuts.
Bill C-136 has weakened the CBC's regional programming role even more. The 1968 Act required the CBC to serve the special needs of geographic regions. Now the Conservatives only want the CBC to reflect Canada and its regions to national and regional audiences. That is a significant difference in responsibility and operation.
Other groups who have spoken to me are very concerned about the policy that fails to ensure a distinction between a made-in-Canada program and Canadian programs made in Canada. There is a very significant difference. The program Night Heat is an example. It is part of a move toward a North American broadcasting system about which we must be very careful as we analyze the impact of this Bill.
The requirement that individual broadcasters provide programming that is predominantly Canadian in character is proposed to be changed. As a result, the CRTC would be free to reduce its requirement that broadcasters maintain 50 per cent Canadian content and still be consistent with the new Bill's intent. The CBC description is reduced to distinctive. These descriptions are of fundamental importance. We see the Bill as paving the way for the Canadian broadcasting system to become more Americanized than we had anticipated.
The CBC's mandate has been altered by removing the requirement that its programming contain a balance of information, entertainment and enlightenment. We are left only with information and entertainment. While programs like Ideas, Quirks <6 Quarks and Arts National on radio and Man Alive and The Nature of Things on television may not attract the large commercial mass audience needed for high ratings and the maximum advertising dollars, it is the kind of programming that has made CBC so unique and highly respected as a broadcaster. The alternative television service is ill-defined.
Broadcasting Act
There are many positive aspects of this Bill. It addresses some areas that needed attention. It was an excellent move to make this Bill technology neutral.
However, there are also issues which makes one wonder about the juxtaposition of the free trade legislation with the broadcasting legislation. I suggest that those considerations will be addressed with great precision under the lens of a microscope.

... to study it through a microscope in order to make sure that the goal the Minister is aiming for is reached, as well as the goal our Committee is aiming for, and the goal of each and every group we have heard, and which the Caplan-Sauvageau Committee has heard, which is to increase the Canadian content of television programs throughout the day so that our children will be able in the future to learn who they are and why they are who they are.
With that observation, I look forward to an open-minded approach at the committee hearings that will take into consideration the observations I read today. These are not my observations but the observations of people who looked at this Bill, people who were part and parcel of the input into this Bill and who are generally happy with the Bill, with the exceptions I have brought to the Minister's attention over the course of the last 37 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, as communications and culture critic for the New Democratic Party, I am very pleased to respond to Bill C-136, to the Minister's speech, and to the speech of my colleague, the Member from the Liberal Party. I think the essential problem with Canadian broadcasting is that the public sector is underfunded and the private sector is not doing its job. I can summarize my speech by that line. I think the rest is detail, although important.
Let me say it again. The public sector under this Government is underfunded. That includes the CBC. The private sector, that is all private radio and television stations especially the television stations, is not doing its job. It is not producing quality Canadian programs. The question is: Will this Bill change the situation? I am afraid that the answer is no, it will not change the situation, all rhetoric aside.
As the Minister has said correctly, this Bill is the first major change to the Broadcasting Act since 1968. The necessity for this change is beyond question and the Minister has also said that. First, for technological reasons there needs to be a change. The evolution of distribution and production technology since 1968 has been truly extraordinary. Just as important, however, a new Act and new policy have been made essential by what might be called the crisis in Canadian broadcasting. That crisis has been the subject of numerous commissioned

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act
reports. If one stacks them up, they would go from the floor to the ceiling. Two of the reports I hold in my hand, the Caplan-Sauvageau report and the report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, are two examples. They outlined the contemporary crisis in Canadian broadcasting, and it is not just because of new technology. The Minister mentioned the satellites and cable that we did not have in 1968. It is a Crisis in watching, if you like. I would like to give some figures from the Caplan-Sauvageau report.

... page 745. Of the 52,000 hours of English-language television programming provided annually to average Canadians, only 70 hours are Canadian drama, including comedies, films, mini-series, etc. Of the 27,000 hours of French-language television programming available to the average francophone viewer, only 630 are Canadian drama. It means that 98 per cent of all English-language drama programs are of foreign origin. For French-language television, the proportion is 90 per cent, Mr. Speaker; only 28 per cent of all programs offered on English-language television are Canadian. Domestically produced programs do not even account for one third of the time Canadians spend watching English-language television.
Francophone teen-agers spend half their television viewing time watching foreign programs. For anglophone teen-agers, the figure is 80 per cent.

Eighty per cent of our Anglophone young people spend their hours in front of television watching foreign programs in English and the majority of the time passed by Francophone young people is also spent watching foreign programming. The crisis of Canadian television is not isolated, and I want to quote from the study by the Caplan-Sauvageau task force:
The reasons for these problems are clear: the public sector, which must be the chief purveyor of quality Canadian programming is inadequately scaled and funded; the private sector which should complement the public sector at least to the extent of contributing to the fulfilment of the social objective of the Broadcasting Act is not contributing enough.
I say also that this crisis, which is documented by the statistics and by the Caplan-Sauvageau report, is not isolated. Canadian television is not isolated in the difficulties we face in developing distinctively Canadian cultural industries. I think the Minister knows this. She is a Canadian nationalist, I believe. She must know that Canadian films represent only 3 per cent of screen time in Canada. Canadian films only take up 3 per cent of our screen time.
Three per cent of film profits stay in Canada. Ninety-seven per cent of profits go outside of Canada. Three per cent of the new video cassette sales are Canadian made. Ninety-seven per cent are foreign made. Our own publishers own only 30 per cent of the Canadian market. Seventy per cent is foreign owned. Seventy-seven per cent of the magazines sold in this country are foreign magazines. Eight-five per cent of the records and tapes sold in this country are foreign. Rick Salutin pointed out: "No other supposedly independent country
mirrors this situation". To be a really independent country, it seems to me that we must have as far as it is possible, and in the sense that we live in a global village, an independent Canadian culture. Frank W. Peers, writing in A Canadian Forum Supplement in March 1988, said:
-one of the tests of nationhood is that more communications take place within a country than between that country and another. Are Canadians governments prepared to recognize the importance of internal communications if the political structure is to be sustained?
I agree that he makes a good point. Doug Fisher, writing in the Toronto Sun-another level of journalism; going from the left to the right here-on June 27, said:
How do you see that the viewers and listeners have their profusion of choice, even as technology widens it, while ensuring enough of the listening and viewing is Canadian to keep our identities and distinctions?
I think that is a good point and I will come back to it. Of course, a wider number of positive things is happening in Canada's cultural industry-and I do not want to sound too negative-in particular with respect to its broadcasting system, with such films as My American Cousin, Un Zoo La Nuit and television programs such as The Kids of Degrassi Junior High. I said before that that is not a description of an evening cabinet meeting.
One sees what Canadian talent can produce. We have lots of talent in Canada. In animation and documentary work, Radio Canada, the CBC, and the National Film Board have had remarkable achievements. One need only draw attention to the work of Frederic Back, whose film L'homme qui plant ait des arbre won an Oscar this year, to see the kind of programs Canadians can produce when given the opportunity. However, it is a little tragic that in the days following Mr. Back's triumph at the Oscars it was revealed that Radio Canada had been forced to dismantle its animation department because of the Government's fierce assault on the budget of French language broadcasting in this country.
What nonsense. He is going to a new international film board.

I should mention the extraordinary success of CBC Radio both in English and French. In spite of being forced to run on a shoe-string it is gaining audiences yearly from the top 40 competitors.
This morning I listened to the Peter Gzowski program. He did a great interview of the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett).
Do you stay in bed that long?

It is a particular shame that due to the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal our ability to engage in such policies will be severely curtailed.
I want to come back to the trade deal because one has to see Bill C-136 in the context of the world around it. Part of the big world around it is the trade deal.
Before leaving this aspect of Canadian culture I want to say that I think we English Canadians do not know how vulnerable we are. I think we cannot wait 20 years for another Broadcasting Act. That is why this Act is so important. In my lifetime we used to have debates, when I was a student, about whether there was a Canadian culture. We meant by that an English Canadian culture. We always felt that there was a French Canadian culture.
There is an English Canadian culture. We have accepted that. We understand it. We know what it is. I do not think that young people today have that debate. There is an English Canadian culture and a French Canadian culture and, above that, a Canadian culture with its multicultural aspects and its native heritage. We know that. The question is: Will we be able to keep that in light of the onslaught of the American empire and its incredible cultural penetration of the Canadian market?
I was told by someone in the Government who is a Francophone, and I will not mention his name, someone who had been in Cabinet: "You Anglophones do not realize that you may lose your whole culture if you do not start now trying to protect it as we in Quebec in the 1960s took measures to protect our culture".
Having outlined the present crisis we face in Canadian broadcasting, I would like to assess what the Government has done over its entire mandate to help or to hinder Canadian broadcasting. I suggest that one cannot look at this new broadcasting policy and at Bill C-136 without putting it into the context of the Government's performance over its mandate.
We have seen the Government over the past four years institute a systematic attack led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on the public broadcasting system in Canada. One need only cite the example of the all-news network decision. In that case the CRTC, the federal regulator, awarded the licence to put together an all-news network to the CBC. The CBC had a bid that was vastly superior to its competitor. It was also cheaper to Canadian subscribers.
The Government and the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) intervened to sabotage the CBC's bid. What is the result of the Government's policy? The result of the Government's policy-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member has made an accusation that he cannot in fact back up in the House. The licence awarded by the CRTC to the CBC for an all-news station comes into effect on
Broadcasting Act
September 1, 1988. The Department of Justice has stated that the appeal period is the 60 days following that. Therefore only then can appeals to the Cabinet be considered.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That sounds a bit like debate.

Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is that right now we do not have an all-news network. The all-news network in Canada is the CNN, Ted Turner's network. We have an American all-news network as a result of the Government's policy in delaying this matter. The real story of the Government's assault on the CBC is found in the vicious budget cuts we have seen over the past four years. I would add that this process started with a previous Liberal Government and has continued. I wish to give Hon. Members the figures.
In 1984-85, the CBC's budget was $905 million. In 1985-86, it was $826 million. In 1986-87, it was $806 million. In 198788, it was $789 million. In 1988-89, it will be $775 million.
With respect to this Bill the Minister talked proudly about the new money for the CBC given to it to help it reach its commendable aim of having 95 per cent Canadian content. In fact, the Minister is giving $20 million to the English service and $15 million to the French service. That is great, but that hardly even begins to correct the damage to public broadcasting the Government has done over the past four years. We cannot, as the Minister apparently believes, continue to expect the CBC to produce magic when it is not given the means to fulfil either its present mandate or the mandate that is outlined in the legislation we are discussing today.
What has been the result of the Government's broadcast policy? We have seen the cut-backs in the CBC budget. There has been de facto privatization of the CBC which is consistently being forced to find new money on its own, mostly through commercials, to make up for its shortfalls. Over the past four years the evolution of CBC generated revenue has been as follows. I will give Hon. Members the figures. In 1984-85, the commercial revenue for the CBC was $232 million. In 198586, it was $232 million. In 1986-87, it was $251 million. In 1987-88, it was $251 million. In 1988-89, it will be $266 million.

Mr. Speaker, the effects of this Government policy have been especially hard on the CBC's French services.

We have seen a pattern. It is: cut the CBC budget and increase commercial revenues for the CBC, force it into becoming more like a private station. The way one makes money, as private broadcasters know, is to bring in all the American cop shows and put them on prime time. That is how cash is generated. That has been the change that this Government is forcing on the CBC.
The Minister said in her speech, and I give her credit for it, that the CBC is the nervous system of our country. When we look not at the Minister's rhetoric but rather examine the

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act
substance of it, we find that it really does not follow this Bill, the letter or the spirit of either the standing committee's report or the Caplan-Sauvageau report. It was not a New Democrat but rather a Conservative, the chairman of the standing committee on broadcasting, who said that 250 million new dollars annually were needed.
The Minister, in relative terms, is offering crumbs to the CBC. Where, at the very least, is the money that was lost by the CBC as a result of the sledge-hammer cuts of the Minister and her predecessor? When it comes to rhetoric the Minister is fine. When it comes to getting the beef, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has not produced it. It is a sham. That is not just my view, Mr. Speaker. I will give Hon. Members some quotes from people who have looked at this matter. The President of ACTRA, Dale Goldhawk, said on June 24, 1988:
And while the CBC is expected to fulfil a wide mandate, the money to go
forward just isn't there. In short, this part of the announcement doesn't
exactly make my socks roll up and down.
The Ottawa Citizen stated:
But MacDonald's pledge to spend $250 million over four years to enhance the Canadian broadcasting system wouldn't even restore funding to the level it was at when the Tories took power four years ago.
And the promised spending is only a fraction of the $130 million to $250 million a year that the all-party communications committee said two weeks ago was necessary to improve the broadcasting system.
MacDonald has obviously won some concessions from a cabinet with a blinding anti-CBC bias. But it didn't buy the basic conclusion of the Caplan-Sauvageau task force ... the CBC is the heart of Canadian broadcasting and it is seriously underfunded.
Jamie Portman stated on June 23 in an article in The Spectator of Hamilton:
The government has ignored a recent call from an all-party Commons committee that it show its commitment to better Canadian programming by increasing its support of broadcasting with up to $250 million in fresh funding annually... in real dollar terms, the CBC's budget has shrunk by more than $ 150 million since the Conservatives came to power.
Mr. Portman is a senior Southam reporter in arts and culture.
Those are my major criticisms with respect to the CBC in this Bill. I have some other matters that I would like to raise about the CBC that should be considered in the legislative committee. We were pleased to find in the Bill, and the Minister acknowledged it, that: "The CBC is the principal vehicle for cultural expression in Canada". We were also pleased that some of the recommendations of the standing committee with respect to the distinctiveness of the French language service and the separation of the president and chairman's office have been addressed.
However, I have the following question for the Minister. As I read the Bill, Clause 91 seems to fire the President of CBC, and no doubt that will be clarified in committee. Clause 91 states:
Every person holding office as a director of the Corporation, other than the President, immediately preceding the coming into force of section 35 shall continue in office-
Goodbye, Mr. Juneau, after that. Perhaps in committee we can examine the difference between the president and how the president is now to be elected by the Board of Directors.
I have some concern, as does my colleague from the Liberal Party, about the word "enlightenment" which has been dropped with reference to the definition section in the Bill. The CBC is expected to become simply a mass audience network with the abandonment of more specialized programming. At the same time, in the Bill the Minister is ignoring the crisis of regional programming in the CBC. On the first point, I would say to the Minister that we need to have a CBC that is capable of having an appeal to a mass audience, while at the same time is able to address more minoritarian interests. To take off the CBC live drama, music, and documentaries, and perhaps programs such as Man Alive, the Minister seems to be making commercial factors the litmus test of what should and should not be on the network.
The real abandonment comes in terms of regional programming. I say to the Minister that we take this very seriously. The standing committee has detailed the problems of regional programming in its report. The CBC has been forced to cut 28 per cent of the resources for regional programming in order to maintain networking programming in recent years. I come from Vancouver and I see what that means to the local CBC, to the actors, the producers, the writers, and the directors. They get laid off.
This Bill reduces the CBC's mandate to meet the distinct needs of the various geographical regions of the country. I do not understand why the Government wants to do this. What we have here is a centralizing of the CBC. If all CBC dramatic programming is to come from Toronto in English and Montreal in French, then this can hardly be called Canadian content totally. The Minister has forgotten that Vancouver, Calgary, Quebec City, Halifax, and Chicoutimi have to be involved in this process in order to have a truly and uniquely Canadian CBC.
The role of enlightenment as well as regional multicultural programming falls under the rubric of the new alternative programming network. However, the Minister has not yet secured the funds for this network. We appreciate that she did not get it turned down, but she put it on hold. We still do not have it. Thus we will have to wait for a few more years of study and delay, and the Government has apparently ruled out a CBC role and left it to the CRTC to decide on the structure. This service does not exist and will not exist until some time in the next decade, yet there is a pressing need for the type of programs that I talked about.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I just want to thank the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) for his comments and clarifications on the situation before us. I accept his comments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Continuing debate with the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway.

Perhaps the House may allow me a few minutes after five o'clock. I was going to finish by five, but if the House will give me a few minutes to wind up I will not abuse it.
I stated that the essential problem with Canadian broadcasting was that the public sector was underfunded. I outlined that in figures and in debate. The second problem was that the private sector was not doing its job. This is probably the weakest part of the Minister's Bill, if I might say so.
In the Bill the Minister proposes to pressure the private network to produce more Canadian programming. This will have, at most, a very modest effect. Private broadcasters are always talking about producing quality Canadian programming, but they show very little interest in providing it. I want to quote from an article in The Vancouver Sun of June 25, 1988. In the article Douglas Sagi quotes Mr. Barry Duggan, Vice-President of CKVU, who stated:
I question whether Canadians want more Canadian programming. But I agree they certainly want better Canadian programming.
This is a standard line. Ray Peters, President of western BCTV, also questioned whether Canadians want more Canadian programs. He stated:
I don't think there should be more Canadian programming. I think there
should be better Canadian programming and that's why I like the idea of
incentives.
That basically summarizes the position of the private sector. The question is: What about the whole idea of this policy thrust? I would like the Minister to pay special attention to this. Robert Fulford, a very distinguished Canadian and writer, has put his finger on it. Mr. Fulford made the point by stating:
-the ancient bureaucratic axiom that an idea should never be allowed to die just because it doesn't work. In this case the idea is that private broadcasters, licensed by a federal regulator to use the public's airwaves, will spend a substantial part of their revenue on original production.
Mr. Fulford basically said that we were flogging a dead horse here. He further stated:
-the parliamentary committee on communications and culture delivered one more rebuke to the broadcasters. "Private television," the committee's report said, "has been making an insufficient contribution to achieving the goals of the Broadcasting Act."
Every royal commission and task force has said the same thing, and each of them-like the parliamentary committee-has then expressed the pious hope that private broadcasters would finally deliver what they promised when they were licensed. Year after year, the broadcasters have declined to
do so-

July 19, 1988
Broadcasting Act
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what the rate of return is for private broadcasters in this country, as set out by the broadcasting committee and not denied by private broadcasters? It averages 50 per cent a year on investment. They are enjoying unprecedented riches, but almost none of this money is going to writers, actors, and film makers. In my view, this Bill is not going to change that.
Private networks have become transmission belts to bring American programs to Canadian viewers with Canadian commercials inserted. The regulators, the CRTC, have not been able to do anything about it over the years. In fact they have become like other regulators an essential part of the business that they are supposed to control.
What is the Government doing to change this matter? It seems that the Government has watered down the requirement in the current Act that private broadcasters be predominantly Canadian-and it has not worked anyway-and has brought in a form of performance incentives.
This is the question I want to put to the Minister, and I was not given unanimous consent to put it. How do these performance incentives work? If you look at it in the face of the Bill, we have fees collected by the Treasury Board if these private networks do not perform with more Canadian content, which they have never done in the past in prime time. This is going to be done in secret. This is a recipe for slush funds, for political interference and for trouble. This is one of the worst parts of the Bill. It is supposedly to attack the worst offender, that is, the private networks especially on television that are using the service just to run American cop shows in Canada, to make a lot of money, and not to put enough of it back into quality Canadian programming. There is the villain.
What are they doing about it? In this Bill the Government is bringing in a very shoddy scheme which is flawed with difficulties in terms of the performance initiatives. I think that we have to look at that issue very deeply in committee.
I want to raise another point and I think the Minister would be interested in it. I want to cover the Bill's reaction to one of the recommendations of the committee with respect to women in minority groups. I will read the recommendation, and I quote:
The programming carried by the system should provide a balanced representation of Canadian society, reflecting its multicultural and bilingual realities, its aboriginal peoples and the composition of its population with respect to sex, age, race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, and mental or physical handicaps.
What does the Bill say in Part I, Section 3? It says the following:
3(l)(a)(iii) strive, through its operations and programming, to reflect the circumstances and aspirations of Canadian men and women, including the linguistic duality and multicultural nature of Canadian society and the special place of aboriginal peoples within that society,
That is not good enough. What the Government said in its reply to the committee about why it could not put in a tough section as the committee recommended was that the goals of commercial expression were to outweigh the goals of government policy toward minority groups and women.
We will still see on television the Italian who is portrayed as greasy, the Newfoundlander who is portrayed as stupid, women who are portrayed as not being important. That kind of continuation of these things will remain on Canadian TV without a tough section. Considering the Minister's record in this matter, she should look at it very carefully.
I see the Minister has arrived, perhaps she did not hear that I was attacking her for the fact that women were very critical of this aspect of the Bill and that that aspect needed strengthening so that the portrayal of women can be different on Canadian television.
With respect to aboriginal communities, I have heard in recent weeks that the Minister's somewhat limited commitment to satellite broadcasting in the North is somewhat less than originally thought. We will be pressing the Government on these proposals. I put it on guard with respect to any weakening of this proposal.
I would like to particularly underline the work of Rosemary Kuptana who is with Television Northern Canada in her proposal. I was co-counsel of the Berger inquiry into the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. In 1974 the CBC, through the vision of the late Andrew Cowan, through the hard work of Whit Fraser, a CBC reporter, and other native reporters, was able to broadcast the hearings in seven languages. That was 1974. We broadcast in English, French, in Dogrib, Slavey, Loucheux, and East and West Arctic Eskimo. That was done. It is amazing what can be done with aboriginal broadcasting in this country. It is amazing what can be done in terms of Canadians from different parts of the country talking to each other. It does not have to be cop shows from L.A. as the basis for Canadian programming.
I want to refer to the trade deal before I close, and why the two matters are so intertwined. Basically the trade deal says that it does not change the status quo. Fine. Then look at the status quo. Three per cent of our film distribution and 80 per cent of our publishing are foreign controlled. We can on down the line. I gave the figures at the beginning of my speech.
What happens if the Minister really wants to change that to enact a nationalistic Canadian policy so that we finally have control of our own airwaves and our own culture? What happens if we want a real progressive policy? Then the other part of the trade deal comes in, the Americans could take equivalent commercial measures, not just in culture but in other aspects like forestry, mining, and so on.
Assume for the moment that you are the Minister of Culture, Mr. Speaker, and that you enact a very progressive policy in which Canadianization is very important and of prime concern. The Americans start retaliating. What do they
July 19, 1988

do? They put tariffs on B.C. lumber or B.C. fish. Then the workers who are out of work come to you and say: "You had better remove that progressive cultural policy".
Do you see how it works, Mr. Speaker? That is the insidious part of the trade deal. The fact is that the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal will mean that there cannot be any Canadian nationalistic cultural policy. There can only be this tinkering that we see in the present Bill, which is fundamentally changing the rules of the game. That is why the people from the Stratford theatre who recently signed a petition of protest, the actors and actresses, know in their hearts that the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal stops the future Canadian Government from really enacting progressive policies with respect to Canadian culture.
I want to end there, because the Bill will go into committee. Marshall McLuhan once said that we lived in a rear-view mirror society. It was like looking in the rear-view mirror in your car, which takes you back to your past. Even though we live in the present we think in the past. Artists, he said, think in the present. They do not live in a rear-view society. We are looking back, it seems to me, in this Bill. We are not looking ahead. The new world means fibreoptics, codable signals on television, and addressable receivers. Nothing has been dealt with in the Bill with respect to that. This is a backward looking Bill, not a forward looking Bill. It is a Bill born in haste, because of the attitude of the Conservatives on pornography, their vicious cut-backs in the CBC, and their general attitude to Canadian cultural agencies and patronage appointments. The Government had to do something, and that is why we are debating this Bill today.
I want to say to the Minister that I am not making those criticisms against her personally. I hold her in the highest of regard. I am sad that she is shackled with such a right wing bunch of Philistines as are in this Government. We have built a unique broadcasting system in Canada. It is unique in that it is ours. It is both public and private. It goes back to many commissions and reports. In the future this new technology will help us. We will have to zero in on choices for Canadians. We do not want to force Canadians to watch Canadian programs. That will not work.
That is exactly what you said earlier.

What we in the NDP offer, which the Government is not offering-and the Liberals have no policy on anything so they are not offering it-is a chance for Canadians to watch quality Canadian programs and for Canadian artists, writers, performers, dancers, and musicians to have those jobs and produce that programming, not only for Canada but for the whole world. To do that there has to be adequate funding for the CBC, including perhaps what Robert Fowler said years ago in his royal commission. He said that we
Broadcasting Act
had to give the CBC a long-term plan and assured funding removed from political influence.
First, we have to fund the CBC adequately and make it the main vehicle of public broadcasting. Second, we have to require private broadcasters to do their fair share. I have my doubts whether the system proposed in this Bill will work.
All you have to do is vote against it.

We cannot wait another 20 years. It is ironic that this debate comes on a Tuesday afternoon in the middle of the summer with a few Members in the House. The Minister is here listening to the debate, I acknowledge that. It is almost like the Bill has gone through as just another Bill. Next to the trade deal it is maybe the most important legislation that we deal with. Let us think of where Canadians spend their time and get their knowledge, Mr. Speaker. They get it through modern communications and from watching TV. That is from where we now pick most of our news, our drama, and public affairs. That is what people do in the modern world. That is why this Bill goes to the whole heart of the future of Canada. That is why this Bill is flawed. It still has not solved the essential problem, and that is an underfunded public sector and a private sector that is not doing its job. That has to be changed or Canadian cultural sovereignty will not survive.
Will the NDP vote against it?
You heard me.
Great.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCOME TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on second reading of Bill C-139, a Bill of vital importance to all Canadians and to the economy of this country. As you know, Bill C-139 concerns the tax reform which started in 1984 and was subsequently continued, a reform that will make our tax system more equitable. First, there was thorough planning.
There was consultation, and adjustments were made as required to provide the majority of Canadians with a tax system responsive to their needs, a system that, I would say,
for the first time in the history of taxation in Canada, responds both to the economic needs of this country and to the needs of Canadian men and women. It is probably the first time, Mr. Speaker, since the famous war tax of 1917, which was a temporary tax, that Canadians will see an increase on their paycheck in July as result of this reform. Mr. Speaker, about 9.7 million Canadian families will pay less income tax in 1988 and subsequent years. This means that 85 per cent of Canadians will pay an average of $500 or less income tax per year. And that is a first!
This was achieved in a number of ways. First, as you know, over the years we phased out the tax shelters provided under the system, such as tax credits for scientific research which meant that billions of dollars were spent by a few taxpayers, a few companies, while the majority of taxpayers did not benefit. And even worse, the people who should have benefited from this scientific research tax credit, our scientists, never benefited at all. It is time we put an end to the abuse that existed under the previous Liberal Government and which cost Canadians billions of dollars without doing anything for our country, without giving Canada anything worthwhile as far as scientific research was concerned. Now that these funds have come back into the system, today we can consider the kind of tax reform that will benefit all Canadians. And as I was saying, 85 per cent of taxpaying Canadians will see their tax bill go down this year-they already saw that on their pay cheque for the beginning of July.
This was also done by broadening the tax base; as you know, many companies were not paying their fair share of taxes, for various reasons. So companies that were not paying tax will from now on pay their fair share, giving us money that will allow us to reduce Canadians' tax burden.
What is perhaps most important in this whole tax reform is the change we made to the personal exemption and all exemptions, converting them into tax credits. As you know, Mr. Speaker, exemptions are beneficial to high-income individuals and penalize low-income Canadians. This is easy to illustrate: If you earn $100,000 a year and have a personal exemption of $3,000, your tax rate is 50 per cent and you save $1,500. But if you earn $10,000 a year, your tax rate is 20 per cent and with the same $3,000 annual exemption, you save $500 or $600 of tax. By changing this and giving everyone the same $1,000 tax credit for personal exemptions, whether they make $10,000 or $100,000 a year, they all have the same tax advantage. And this is a major reform of our tax system. It makes it an equitable system, fairer for all Canadians. Looking at my colleague from Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), I am sure that he cannot contradict this. He is familiar enough with the tax system to know that tax credits definitely make our system fairer and more equitable. This same principle will apply to all exemptions that Canadians had before, like the married exemption, etc.
July 19, 1988

Tax reform also has another purpose, namely to encourage private initiative, to give Canadians more money in their pocket, as we have been saying since 1984, so that they can decide what to do with it. I do not think that it is up to the Government to direct everything that goes on in the daily lives of all Canadians. The more money taxpayers have in their pockets, the more they will be able to spend as they like, or save or invest, spend on recreation, whatever; that will be good for our economy and our country. And it will automatically encourage economic growth and help create jobs. That is how you have to look at tax reform; this is the philosophy for Canada's future to keep in mind.
Our reform will also solve the problem of corporate taxation. Some companies were overtaxed and others paid nothing at all. As I said, those that paid nothing will pay from now on. But those that were overtaxed could not be internationally competitive; again, Mr. Speaker, in running a country, you must not think only of tomorrow, but 5, 10, 11 years ahead. We are 11 years away from 2000. This underscores the importance of the free trade agreement and of the tax reform which will make Canadian companies more competitive on international markets because their tax rates will indeed stand comparison with those of companies in other countries. It is just as important to Canadians who want to work, who have jobs and want to hang on to them, who are eager to make progress and seek to achieve a better quality of life. You know, Mr. Speaker, very often people equate quality of life with environmental considerations. It is true and it is a sound approach. I think in terms of social benefits, it is true and it is a sound approach as well. But quality of life also implies that Canadians have decent incomes which are not reduced by unduly high taxes. There are no incomes without jobs, and there will be jobs only if Canadian companies can make progress and expand on a logical, normal and lasting basis. That is where that tax reform comes in.
Viewed from a different angle, the reform means that
850.000 Canadians will no longer pay income taxes. Low income Canadians will no longer be taxpayers, including
250.000	older men and women who will never again have to file a tax return, if indeed they have no other income to declare.
With respect to older Canadians, the tax reform means that nine out of ten of them will pay less income tax. Mr. Speaker, you can appreciate that the one out of ten who will have to pay more has a much higher income, and it is only normal that he or she contributes to our society just like all other Canadian men an women.
We have maintained the $100,000 capital gains tax exemption, $100,000 which again will make it possible for Canadian taxpayers to invest and earn a fair investment income.
As a rule, as you know, investments create a great many jobs. So we left at $500,000 the capital gain exemption to benefit farmers as well as small and medium sized businesses.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
In this country, most jobs are created by small and mediumsized businesses, and I think it is advisable, as well from an economic point of view in terms of the tax reform, to give special attention to those who keep the economy moving and create employment. That is the reason the $500,000 capital gain exemption exists for them.
And the same reform offers the advantage of being an incentive for the private industry. I met last weekend with people with small and medium-sized businesses who told me: we feel it is important for our employees to have a lighter tax burden because we can give them a good pay, and it is equally important that our business should also have a lighter tax burden to keep us competitive on the international market.
Mr. Speaker, the future of Canadian businesses is on the international market. I do not think that as Canadian businessmen, we should rest on our laurels but that we should think of the future. We must realize that we have in Canada some 25 million potential consumers, but we should think of the new opportunities open to us. In the Trois-Rivieres riding, there are a number of very good business people who have already understood the message and who are already exporting in large quantities on the international market. I could mention a few who, through their exports, have created dozens upon dozens of new jobs in my riding. If these people had felt that they were going to limit themselves to Trois-Rivieres, the region, the province or even the country, fewer jobs would have been created in Trois-Rivieres. I feel I must congratulate and encourage our Canadian exporters to look towards this extraordinary new market which beside the United States- this will be achieved through the Free Trade Agreement-also includes the European Common Market. We must have an economic vision of what will happen in a few years from now and to take the necessary steps in Canada to improve the quality of life for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I referred a moment ago to a vision of the future. Automatically, we think of children. The child's tax credit in 1988 has reached $559 and is consistent with what we had already announced in 1986 concerning the federal sales tax.
You will certainly remember that when we increased the federal sales tax by 1 per cent in 1986, we introduced at the same time the concept of a sales tax credit for low-income people and families.
That is what I called developing a tax system which takes into account the needs of Canadians, something foreign to the former Liberal Government which increased taxes without an eye for the future. We had ample evidence of this with the successive budgets of the previous federal government, the scientific research tax credit, the various industries where they abused the income tax legislation, overburdened Canadian taxpayers, without ever doing anything to improve the quality of life and the economic future of Canada.
This is a priority of the tax reform, something for which we can congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and

July 19, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
say: You have done a great job! The tax reform is great for all individual Canadian taxpayers, for all Canadian corporations, for the economy of Canada and the quality of life of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite may quack as much as he pleases, nothing he can say will disprove that. Those are the facts of Canadian tax reform.
I see my colleague from Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) nodding that I am right. Even though he is on the other side of this House, he's able to recognize-because he is an honest man-the good things accomplished by the Conservative Government, and I congratulate him for it.
It might be useful, Mr. Speaker, while talking about tax reform, to go back to what has been done since 1984. With the minimum tax put in place in 1986, for example, all Canadians must pay their fair share. That could have been done under the previous Liberal Government, but their good friends wouldn't stand for it. We have put in place a system that requires all Canadian taxpayers to pay their taxes on a yearly basis.
We have also stopped income splitting between family members, which provided tremendous tax shelters to restricted groups. That has also been set aside.
The Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan was primarily used as a tax shelter by families, but low income people couldn't afford to take advantage of it. That has also been settled.
Tax shelters created by the old regime for yachts, cottages and the like were used any which way. We also put a stop to that.
The scientific research tax credit, which I referred to earlier, cost Canadians billions of dollars, didn't do anything for our scientists or the Canadian economy, but fattened some companies' pocketbooks. That, Mr. Speaker, is an aberration. It is unbelievable that this party let such things go by when it was in power.
I recently read an article in which the former Minister of Finance said that he was aware of what was going on but that nothing could be changed and that the deed was done. So they let it go at that. They let billions of dollars escape which should have gone to companies X, Y, Z here in Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, when we speak of fiscal reform, I think we must also consider the second stage of fiscal reform. Indeed, it is also important. It is part of the vision of Canada, of the expectation of a better quality of life which I mentioned earlier.
The second stage of fiscal reform will deal with the federal sales tax. It is a well known fact that the federal sales tax, in its present patchwork form, in its sorry state which defies description, Mr. Speaker, and with which the former Liberal administration had managed to "put up", is a nuisance to Canadian businesses and prevents them from competing successfully with foreign firms.
So the second stage is on its way and hopefully, as negotiations are proceeding well, with the agreement of the ten provinces we shall arrive at one single provincial and federal sales tax which will apply to most if not all goods and whereby Canada as well as the ten provinces will have a better tax system for the good of all Canadians, one which will be beneficial, which will improve the quality of life of Canadians and, rather than cause the loss of jobs in Canada, will create employment as does the first part of the tax reform, which I hope will be adopted as soon as possible by this House.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity which we get very seldom, to put questions in the House to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, in this case on matters concerning tax reform.
Mr. Speaker, despite the fact that the tax reform proposal was tabled in the House in June 1987, today, July 19, 1988, is the first time we debated the issue in the House, except for a few short statements in response to the statements made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in June and December last year.
I have a question for the Parliamentary Secretary. He just said that all Canadians should pay their fair share of taxes, but in the Government's proposal, and I have the figures here, we see that among the winners, a family with an annual income of $100,000 will enjoy a tax reduction of $4,165 compared with $140 for the individual with an annual income of less $15,000.
Mr. Speaker, the Government seems to think that those who were not paying their fair share were mainly Canadians on low incomes. If we look at the breakdown, we see that the 26 per cent on low incomes will receive about $250 million in tax deductions, but the 2 per cent on higher incomes will get about $380 million in tax deductions. This means that 12 per cent of these reductions go to the wealthier groups in our society and only 8 per cent to people on low incomes, despite the fact that the latter group is much bigger.
Could the Parliamentary Secretary explain why the Government failed to introduce a tax reform proposal that would provide for a more progressive tax system? If we consider all taxpayers, in both cases the winners, that is those who are well off, receive far more in terms of tax reductions than those on low incomes. And could he explain the fact that if we consider the principle of fair tax treatment of families and single taxpayers, there seems to be a disparity that is indefensible in terms of social and fiscal justice? Mr. Speaker, a taxpayer with an annual income of $30,000 and who happens to be single receives a tax reduction of $695 per year, but if we have two taxpayers, both working with two children, their tax reduction is only $285.
July 19, 1988

It is difficult to give all the figures, but I wonder why a family with two wage earners who both have to work to be able to pay the rent or their mortgage, receive about $5 per week in tax reductions, while someone else with the same annual income will get $14 per week in tax reductions; and why do the wealthy get thousands of dollars in tax reductions, while those who are less well off might get a few hundred dollars? Why?
