Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the questions the socialists ask are always distorted and do not reflect reality. What I said at the beginning was that those who paid no tax will pay. And those who paid no tax, those who did not pay their fair share, were the ones who benefited from the tax shelters introduced by the previous Liberal Government. There are no more tax shelters. All Canadians must pay their fair share. There are no more tax shelters and the minimum tax was introduced for the very purpose of making everyone pay his or her fair share.
Moreover, 850,000 Canadians will no longer pay income tax. Eighty-five per cent of Canadians will pay less income tax. But still, Mr. Speaker, the socialist Member is unhappy. Eighty-five per cent of Canadians will pay less income tax and he is not happy! Eight hundred fifty thousand Canadians will no longer pay a cent of income tax. He is still not happy!
It was the same socialist Member, Mr. Speaker, who said that flow-through shares, which are a tax shelter, as you know, should be kept. This same Member is telling us to cut tax shelters and not to give to the rich and those with high incomes. Mr. Speaker, it is high-income individuals who buy flow-through shares; not people with low incomes, but those with high incomes buy them. So you see what the socialist Member is doing, Mr. Speaker. He is speaking out of both sides of his mouth. That is quite unfortunate. We have a fair, equitable tax reform that will benefit most Canadians and that will also . . . but the socialist Member does not mention that, nor that we have converted exemptions into tax credits, which definitely makes the tax system fairer than it was before. He does not talk about that. But maybe he should take a look at it, maybe he should take a proper look at his figures, and he would then see that this is fairness, this is a Government that shoulders its responsibilities and also considers the country's economy. You have to have a vision of the country when you carry out a reform, and a vision of the country for the future also, for the future of Canadians and their children. That is what the tax reform does.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate on this Bill on tax reform. Tax reform was introduced with great fanfare by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It was introduced as being his effort to simplify the tax system.
When I first saw the Bill I asked: Is it not great that we have a simple tax system? I decided to read some of this simple Bill, which has only 500 pages, since it introduces a new simplified tax system. I want to read some of it into the record to show how simple it is and how Canadians will be glad that the tax system has been simplified in this manner. It states at page 149:

We have had some deliberations on this Bill at the committee level. On May 17, 1988,1 attended the Finance Committee hearing because I was interested in this new simplified tax system. In his excellent speech earlier today, Mr. Speaker, the Flon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) explained to the House that this tax reform occurs following four major tax increases from this Tory Government. We should remember
that these increases were quite unfair for middle-income Canadians. And we know that under this tax reform, there will be very little progressiveness in the application of this so-called reform. The reform is certainly incomplete, because the sales tax will be delayed until next year. But why next year? The answer is quite simple and most Canadians are aware of it: because this Tory government wants to implement these tax increases only after the election. Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is something which this Tory Government has overlooked but which you know as well as I do, being non-partisan, and it is that the forthcoming election will mean the end of this Tory Government. That is fortunate for most Canadians, except of course for the rich friends of this Tory Government.
Mr. Speaker, the personal income tax under the proposed tax reform will be reduced from 10 to 3. So the federal tax rate will be 17 per cent on the first $27,500 of taxable income, 26 per cent on the amount between $27,500 and $55,000 in taxable income, and finally 29 per cent on the amount in excess of $55,000 in taxable income. If you look at the three levels, you see quite clearly 17, 26 and 29. Therefore, the middle class will face a tax rate of 26 per cent. Mr. Speaker, 26 per cent is not halfway between 17 per cent and 29 per cent. As you can see, people with average salaries will again pay more than their fair share, contrary to what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister explained to us today. Again, this is a Tory legislation which is unfair to a great many Canadians.
The Parliamentary Secretary told us today something to the effect that the affluent in Canada should assume their fair share of the tax burden. That is true and most of us agree that the rich should pay their share and naturally low income people should not have to shoulder a disproportionate amount of the tax burden. Well, we are well aware that ever since this Tory Government came to power, 1 million Canadians are paying more income tax. The Government is now saying that 850 000 Canadians will pay less income tax. Well, Mr. Speaker, the net result is that 150 000 Canadians will continue to pay more. If 1 million pay more while 850 000 pay less, the net result is that 150 000 Canadians are already losers in this whole process, even before the implementation of Phase 2 of this Tory Government's tax reform. The end result is that Canadians are always losing under a Tory Government. It is a well known fact that Tory times are hard times. As the English say .. .

Tory times are hard times. Let me remind Canadians of some of the tax increases. Since the Tories have came to power, many Canadians are paying more income tax. As I indicated previously, a million taxpayers are paying more.
Let me refresh the memories of Members of the House and all Canadians who are listening to us with respect to those tax increases. First, let me talk about direct taxes. In October 1984 we had a sales tax increase from 9 per cent to 10 per cent, a $1 billion increase. On January 1, 1986, the sales tax increased from 10 per cent to 11 per cent, another $1 billion
July 19, 1988

tax increase. As the Tories say: "What is a billion?" On April 1, 1986, the sales tax increased from 11 per cent to 12 per cent, another $1 billion. Then they decided to extend the tax to children's candy-Tory policy-soft drinks, health goods, dental instruments, snack foods, and so on. That resulted in $460 million of tax increase. There was an increase in sales tax from 8 per cent to 12 per cent on paint, wallpaper, and children's toys, which produced $60 million.

Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), to be turfed out in 1979. That is the sad reality.
Unfortunately for all Canadians this particular Conservative administration has a large majority in the House of Commons. What I am saying today must be thought provoking. It is even waking up some of the Tory back-benchers. That is a good sign. They are earning their day's pay.

He imposed a sales tax not on basic service, not on luxury items, but on long-distance telephone calls, which means that this tax is unfair and discriminatory against the rural Canadians I am charged with representing in the House of Commons. That is the unfairness of this system and this so-called tax reform with these tax increases of the Conservative administration.
I see the Hon. Member for Gaspe (Mr. Marin) opposite. He represents, as I do, a rural riding. He knows how unfair are those taxes on long-distance telephone calls. He has probably had the opportunity to tell the Minister of Finance. If he has not had that opportunity, there is still some time before the Tories are turfed out of office; a few months at least but not much more. He should tell the Minister of Finance, while he is still the Minister of Finance, that this tax on long-distance telephone calls is indeed unfair to a large number of rural

Canadians living in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and elsewhere.
It is particularly unfair to senior citizens. I received a telephone call yesterday in my office from a senior citizen in my riding who, upon looking at his telephone bill, became really upset about the fact that because he lives in Hawkes-bury he had to pay tax on a long-distance phone call to his children living in Ottawa. He has to pay surtax because he has cablevision coming into his house. This gentleman is 88 years old. Why is the Government permitted to impose these types of taxes on senior citizens such as the one I have just described? Obviously there is no rational explanation for that other than the fact that the Minister of Finance is insensitive to the needs of rural Canadians. He has imposed this most unfortunate regressive and discriminatory tax on rural Canadians, the tax on long-distance telephone calls.
There are pages of tax increases in the Bill. I could read them all into the record but if I did that I could hardly speak on anything else this afternoon, except of course if my colleagues extended the time permitted for me to speak, which I know that given the non-partisan tone of my speech they would probably want to do. In the unlikely event that they refuse, I am going to change topics here and move on to more on the area of tax reform.
In the constituency that I represent there is an organization which builds low-head generating stations. These generating stations create employment in my constituency. They are then built on site. They are manufactured in my riding and installed in northern Ontario. They usually provide meaningful employment to residents of remote communities in northern Ontario. This was creating good employment in my riding, which is certainly not in northern Ontario but which suffers from high unemployment. People investing in these types of projects were doing so by means of the flow-through share mechanism. Of course, they have now had a lot of difficulty, first, with the outright cancellation of this measure and, second, with the modifications that were proposed by the Minister of Finance. The long and short of it is that valuable research, development and installation was going on here, and now the whole thing has been placed in jeopardy by the actions of the Conservative administration.
We know that the New Democratic Party has had a great deal of difficulty with this issue. Sometimes it has been in favour of it and sometimes it has been against it. It has not been easy for members of that Party, and I sort of sympathize with them on this issue. I will return to the area of research and development in a minute.
I want briefly to touch on the area of automobile expenses in the tax reform Bill. A number of people in my constituency and several other constituencies in Canada use their cars to work. Their car is a travelling office. I feel that the imposition of the $20,000 maximum for the deductibility of automobiles

Income Tax Act and Related Acts
is unfair. I ask the Minister at least to index that amount and, hopefully, even to increase it so that it will not adversely affect people who work in their cars.
If one's office does not have wheels on it, then it is fully deductible. If an office does have wheels on it, as is the case with a travelling salesperson, then there are restrictions which are unfair which have been put on them by the Government.
In conclusion, I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative Government has failed miserably in the area of research and development with or without tax reform. I talked about the flow-through shares. There are several other areas which I could address.
I want to say that in the United States the non-tax support for research and development is 33 per cent and the tax support is 7 per cent for a total of 40 per cent. In France there is 22 per cent non-tax support and 7 per cent tax support for a total of 29 per cent. In Canada, we have 12 per cent non-tax support and 8 per cent tax support for a total of 20 per cent. We can see how underfunded research and development is in Canada.

That the amendment be amended by deleting the "and" before (6) and the

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words in support of Bill C-139 which deals with the question of tax reform. You and I, Mr. Speaker, have heard a lot about tax reform over quite a number of years. In fact, when I first considered standing for Parliament, I can remember that the whole issue of tax reform was in the forefront of public discussion and debate. I can remember a leadership contender in our Party by the name of Mr. Peter Pocklington who made that one of the prime objectives and thrusts of his efforts to become the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party in 1983. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, the debate that raged around the issue of tax reform. As a nominated candidate for office, knocking on the doors of many people, I found a great interest in and a great desire for tax reform.
However, tax reform means different things to different people. As we talk to different people, they send us the message that tax reform does not always mean the same to everybody. If there is one thing that people have in common about tax reform, it is the whole question of its conveying the meaning to them that they will be paying less taxes under some sort of reformed system than they were under the present or past system. That is what the Bill before us this evening is all about. This Bill means that Most people will pay less in tax than they have been paying.

July 19, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
I had the opportunity of sitting here today and listening to the comments of the Opposition with respect to this Bill. I listened to the Elon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) speaking on behalf of the Liberals. I listened to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) speaking on behalf of the NDP-the new dinosaur Party. I also listened to the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). Frankly, as I listened to their comments, I was astounded. I wondered if we were talking about the same thing. I have a friend who was the Mayor of the Borough of East York where I hail from by the name of Leslie Saunders. He used to describe some things as being "out of this world". As I listened to the comments of the Liberals and the new dinosaurs, I had to agree with him that they were "out of this world". In fact, I thought that perhaps they were "out of this world" by many of the comments they made on tax reform. I could spend all my time commenting on all of the things that they said. However, I do want to comment on a few of the things, because they were and they are "out of this world".
One of the first comments the Liberals made had to do with the question of the progressiveness of the income tax system. Both Liberal Members who spoke in this debate indicated that under the former Liberal Governments there was a progressive tax system but that for some reason or other, the progressive tax system is now being done away with. Well, I can see the smile curving at the edges of your mouth when you hear those words about the progressive tax system under the former Liberal Governments. You and I know about all of those interesting tax shelters that the former Liberal Government had introduced and put into effect. You will remember the tax shelter for MURBs. That certainly was a very progressive measure. It allowed people with high incomes to invest their money and in fact to have a tax deduction and not pay any tax on the money that they had in that tax shelter.
You will remember, of course, the film investment tax shelters that were put in place by the former Government, again a tax shelter which enabled rich people to invest their money in the production of movies, shelter their income and not pay any income tax on it.
You will remember as well that there were similar tax shelters for things like hotel investments, similar tax shelters for things like recreational vehicle purchases. These certainly added to the progressiveness of the tax system in a big way. You know that as well as I do that the system that was in place under the former Liberal Government was anything but a perfect progressive tax system.
To top it all off, there was something called the scientific research tax credit, one of the greatest boondoggles that has ever been introduced into the income tax system by any Government. It was introduced by the former Liberal Government, and it milked and looted the Treasury of this country. It certainly could not be considered in any way, shape or form to
be adding to the progressiveness of the tax system. In fact, it did just the opposite, as all of these tax shelters did.
What has happened to these tax shelters, as you and I know, is that they have been eliminated by the present Government, by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and all of those steps in eliminating those tax shelters have helped to return the system to a progressive tax system, the kind of a system that the Liberals tell us that they want to see but the kind of a system that certainly they did not produce.
Another of the comments of the Liberal spokesman on this tax reform legislation had to do with the question of the simplicity of the tax system. Once again the Liberal spokesman seemed to imply that the tax system as it existed under the previous Government was far simpler than it is going to be under the present system.
You and I know that many of the complications of the previous system-complications which included some of these tax shelters-are being eliminated by the present Government. One thing that always strikes me about this whole question of simplicity-and several members of the Opposition have touched on this issue, whether they were Liberals or new dinosaurs-is that it seems to imply that it is some sort of a panacea, that there is some way of creating a simple system but still creating the same kind of a system that they want to see, one which takes into account rich Canadians, poor Canadians, and the question of a progressive tax rate. You and I know that that is very difficult and probably impossible to accomplish.
Certainly we can have a simple system, one where all of us can sit down, as we did 40 or 50 years ago, and work out our income tax on one simple page, but it does not take into account all of the complexities that have now been built into the system, which would cause a great furore and uproar if they were done away with.
One simple example, is the deductions for charitable donations. You know, Mr. Speaker, as I know, that under that very simple system that we used to have there was no such thing as making deductions for charitable purposes from income tax. That system was instituted in an effort to assist organized charities to raise money. A great number of organized charities doing very beneficial work for society have been created under that system.
Just think, Mr. Speaker, of the furore the Opposition would raise if we suddenly did away with the charitable donation or any charitable tax credit whatsoever. Certainly it would make the system much simpler, but at the same time it would devastate this system of charitable giving and the system of charitable expenditures that have been built up over many years. It would make the system simpler, but it certainly would devastate the present charitable scheme that has been established over many, many years.
Another comment of both of the opposition Parties had to do with the fact that although the Government has indicated
July 19, 1988

that there are some 850,000 taxpayers who will be taken off the tax rolls by this tax reform legislation, in fact there are a million people who are now paying taxes that were not when the Government took office.
Again, Mr. Speaker, you and I know that there is a very simple answer to that, and that is the fact that when the Government took office, there was an unemployment rate across this country of something approaching 12 per cent, whereas that has now been lowered very substantially.

Into the 7 per cent range. You and 1 know, Mr. Speaker, that most of those people who are new taxpayers are people who were not working before but now have jobs. No wonder they are paying taxes. I guess they are happy to do that. They were not happy when they did not have a job. They wanted a job, and they knew that with a job they would have to pay some income tax. That is in fact what has happened.
As you know, there have been over 1.2 million new jobs created since September, 1984. In fact, it is interesting to note that unemployment has fallen since 1984 by 430,000. The number of unemployed youth has fallen by 201,000. The number of unemployed women has fallen by 150,000. That means, very simply, that these people now have jobs which they did not have before. It is no wonder that they are paying taxes where they were not paying taxes before.
The Opposition in their criticism went on to deal with a number of other items as well. One of the things that they talked about was the unfairness of things like the capital gains tax exemption and the dividend tax credits. In a recent newsletter I published an outline of how this new tax reform legislation would impact on the average taxpayer. I published in effect a tax return for 1988, and I left it to the reader to work out their own income tax in terms of that income tax return for 1988. I invited them to contact me if in fact they were going to have to pay more tax or have to pay less tax. It is interesting to note that 100 per cent of the people who contacted me and who felt that they were going to have to pay more tax under this system were either people in a high-income bracket to begin with or people who were presently taking advantage of the dividend tax credit, whether they were modest-income people or whether they were high-income people, and it is that that concerned them.
Some modifications had been made to this legislation which the NDP says is helping the rich get richer. Those modifications concern people with high incomes because with the changes in the dividend tax credit and the change from what was anticipated in the capital gains tax credit, they anticipated that they would be paying less income tax with the present system than they would be with the new system. It is significant to my mind, Mr. Speaker, that these so-called assists to the rich, the dividend tax credit and the capital gains tax credit, are really the main source of criticism on the income
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
tax reform package. People in the higher income tax brackets feel the substantial change in the tax system and feel they will be paying much more tax than they paid in the past whereas I, at least, am not hearing from the lower income people because, I assume, having worked out their tax, they find that they are saving money. It is not costing them any money under the new system.
Finally, let me comment on the criticism which the opposition Parties have levied regarding the sales tax changes. The opposition Parties said that people are now paying tax on potato chips but were not before. I have a company in my constituency by the name of Wrigley's Gum. Wrigley's Gum became very exercised with me and with the Government a couple of years ago when it discovered that under the sales tax system people who bought Wrigley's Gum had to pay sales tax whereas those people who bought potato chips did not.
The Wrigley's Gum people felt that potato chips were a direct competitor to them and said that everybody should be paying sales tax on goods or no one should be paying sales tax. I suppose the Government could have said: "Well, we will eliminate sales tax on everything". As you know, Mr. Speaker, that would have meant tax on something else.
Another comment which the opposition Members have made and make regularly has to do with the whole question of the increases in taxation over the last four years. There is one simple answer. Under the previous Government, supported by the New Democratic Party, the deficit in this country rose enormously to frightening heights, approaching $40 billion on an annual basis. When our Government came to office, we started off by suggesting we would cut some of the expenditures so as to reduce the deficit. Every single solitary suggestion that was made for a cut was opposed vehemently by the Liberals and by the new dinosaur party. In each case, both opposition Parties opposed anything that would cut expenditures and now, of course, they are opposing and have opposed anything that would change the tax system in any way. You know, Mr. Speaker, and I know that when you are in Government you cannot have it both ways. Unfortunately, the Opposition wants to imply that you can have it both ways. That just does not work and we all know it. Even the opposition Parties know it in their hearts.
I did not hear the Opposition commenting on the results of tax reform. The Government has said that the net personal income tax revenues to the Government will be reduced under this package by about $12 billion over the next five years. I did not hear either of the opposition Parties dispute that in any way. The federal Government said the income taxes will be reduced for 9.7 million households for over 85 per cent of all households by an average of $490. I did not hear either of the opposition Parties or any of the opposition spokesmen dispute those facts.
The Government says that about 850,000 low income Canadians will have their income tax rates reduced to zero or will receive refundable tax credits in 1988. I did not hear

July 19, 1988
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
either of the opposition Parties or their spokesmen dispute those facts. The Government said that income taxes will be cut for about 1.3 million of the 1.4 million households. About
250,000	elderly Canadians will have their income taxes reduced to zero. I did not hear either opposition Party dispute that nor any of their spokesmen dispute those facts.
All in all, it is interesting to note that as the Government has indicated, under this tax reform package there will be a very substantial reduction. In fact, a very, very substantial number of people will be cut off the tax rolls entirely. A very, very substantial number of people will have their taxes reduced, but we did not hear any of those facts disputed. All we heard disputed was the past. That is where both opposition Parties stand on this issue and on all issues. They are deeply rooted in the past. They do not seem to be able to look forward or get their heads out of the sand. It is time that both opposition Parties admitted, as they know in their hearts, that this is good legislation. It will be good for Canadians and we should see the Bill passed quickly.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for his speech. I found it a bit difficult listening to him to recognize how progressive his Party really was. I noted the number of people whose taxes would be cut. I do not dispute the figures particularly, but what I noted was that a cut, after you have had a big increase, is hardly a cut at all. It reminds me of the story of somebody who goes to the store and he or she-I will be catholic about this-comes back and says: "Well it was 33 per cent off. I could not afford to buy it". You still wind up paying something for whatever it is you bought. That is very much the same with Conservative tax reform.
If your taxes go up by $1,500, which is what has happened for the average family since 1984 under the Conservatives, and you get a tax cut of $300, should you be grateful for the tax cut or should you not recognize the fact that you still wind up paying $1,200 or more in taxation compared to when the Government came to power. That seems to me a very relevant figure. I do not think it is a very progressive type of tax reform if the Conservatives wind up soaking the average family $1,200 more after four years and after tax reform than that family was paying before.
I heard the Hon. Member trying to blame the Opposition that the Conservatives could not cut expenditures where they felt like cutting expenditures. We make up 32 Members in the House of Commons. There are a few more Liberals, a total of some 70 Members in Opposition. The Progressive Conservative Party has three times our number. If they could not cut expenditures, it was because they did not know how, they did not want to, or it was politically unfeasible.
However, my question is whether it is progressive, in his view, to cut taxes on the average person earning more than $100,000 a year to a level lower than in 1984, but to raise taxes on all other Canadians higher than they were in 1984? Is it progressive to have three-quarters of the taxpayers earning over $100,000 a year receiving a tax cut of $4,165, whereas the average taxpayer earning under $15,000 a year gets a cut of only $140? If he thinks that is progressive, I am not in agreement with him and I find it very difficult to associate myself with the so-called tax reform put forward by his Party. It is not fair reform, it is Tory tax reform.
The Hon. Member suggested his Party had done away with a number of tax shelters and therefore deserved a certain amount of praise. He neglected to mention the $100,000 total tax break for capital gains which is available largely to high income Canadians. Is that not a tax shelter worthy of being enshrined in the pantheon of Liberal tax shelters which the Conservative Government inherited? If that is the case, why did the Government, if it is so progressive, not eliminate it?
I would conclude by saying that since the Hon. Member insists on referring to my Party by a name unfamiliar to me, and I always thought the dinosaurs were in the Progressive Conservative Party, and given the retrogressive nature of the tax reform proposed by the Progressive Conservatives, they should be renamed the "prehistoric coprolite party".

Mr. Speaker, I definitely wish to participate in this debate this evening. I might say, however, being a member of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, that we have discussed tax reform for almost two years now and it is not until the dying months of the Government, in the middle of the summer, that it finally brings in its legislation. It seems to me the Government has waited for some of its most important legislation in order to try and ram it through Parliament when at least half of the Members are not present and most Canadians are either on holidays or at the cottage. I think the Government's intention is quite clear. It is not interested in the Canadian people having too close a look at what is in the legislation, and I do not think it is interested in having a full debate in the House on this legislation.
When we first heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) about tax reform, he stated in his speech on June 18, 1987, page 7360 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I am proposing sweeping changes to Canada's tax
system. These changes will directly affect all Canadians for many years to
come.
Our tax system should be a strong force in meeting the challenges that face
our country.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
It must help individuals and businesses deal with the challenges of the 1990s and into the next century.
It must reinforce our ability as a country to continue to provide the social programs needed by our people.
It must generate the hope and opportunity that will motivate Canadians to build a strong country in a very competitive world.
But to do this, the tax system must have the respect of Canadians. We know that it does not. And we know why.
We all know that the tax system allows many profitable corporations to avoid paying a fair share of tax, year after year.
We all know that it allows some people with very high incomes to pay less tax than the average Canadian wage earner, year after year.
We all know that it allows those who are able to use special tax breaks to shift the burden to others less able to carry it.
Canada needs a tax system that raises revenues in a fair and reliable way; a system that supports our national effort to promote economic growth and create more and better jobs.
Those were the comments of the Minister of Finance. By these comments I and all Canadians will judge the legislation before us today.
Since the Conservatives were elected, corporate income tax has increased by 8 per cent, personal income tax has increased by 45 per cent and sales tax has increased by a whopping 67 per cent. I ask again, is this equity, is this fairness? It is obvious to the Canadian public that the tax burden, particularly under a Conservative Government, has been placed on the shoulders of income earners, mainly the middle-income earners. They are the ones who are carrying an increasing load of the tax burden. Again, corporate income tax has only increased by 8 per cent since the election of the Government but personal income tax has increased by 45 per cent and the sales tax has increased by 67 per cent.
Conservative Members, including the Minister of Finance, made much to do about how this tax reform proposal will take some 850,000 low-income earners off the tax rolls. They are right, but they do not mention that since the election of this Tory Government some one million low-income Canadians have been put on the tax rolls. What we have is a revolving door, smoke and mirrors. The Government made low-income Canadians liable to pay tax and is now taking some of them off the rolls. However, that is only temporary because the Government failed to reintroduce full indexation and many of the 850,000 Canadians taken off the income tax rolls this year will be back on next year or the year after.
One million Canadians were put on the income tax roll because the Government took away indexation. Therefore, as incomes rose, because of inflation, they all of a sudden found themselves paying tax whereas before the election of this Government at least the thresholds kept pace with inflation. The Government took that away and that is why one million Canadians who should not be paying taxes because of their low incomes are paying tax for the first time. The Government is now attempting to take credit for removing 850,000 of them for this year only. I emphasize the fact that it is for this year

only because full indexation has not been introduced and many of these 850,000 low-income Canadians will be paying tax again next year or the year after.
The Minister talks about fairness, he talks about removing the tax load from the backs of poor and middle-income people. I ask again whether he has done it. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that he has not. He has reduced the rates of wealthy Canadians from a top rate of 51 per cent to 44 per cent. In other words, a stockbroker earning $200,000 a year is going to save $15,000. Is it fair that a secretary earning $28,000 per year should have a marginal tax rate 5 per cent lower than someone earning over $1 million a year? Is is equity that a secretary or labourer earning $28,000 a year should have an effective tax rate only 5 per cent lower than a person earning over $1 million a year?
What we have before us today is a sham. Let us look again at the savings. A household earning $15,000 a year saves $90 with this tax reform proposal. A household earning up to $100,000 a year saves $1,615 in taxes. A household earning over $100,000 will save $4,365 per year in taxes.
Is this fairness? Is this equity? It is not, it is a sham. It is a sham that the Tories are hoping to perpetrate on the Canadian public. I suspect that the average savings in income tax of $8 per week which the average Canadian received on his pay cheque in the month of July will not make up for the many tax increases that the Government has imposed on many of those Canadians.
One should also mention that much of these income tax savings will be lost. In fact, most of it will be lost because of the increases in sales tax which the Government has introduced for this year. There is a $1.1 billion increase in sales taxes for 1988. Therefore, most of the poor will lose out.
When the Minister of Finance announced his tax reform proposals, he also mentioned that many Canadians have lost respect for the tax system because many large corporations did not pay any tax. In his White Paper he stated that in the year 1983, 110,000 profitable corporations did not pay a cent of tax. He was proud to point out that had his proposals been in effect, some 50,000 of those corporations would now be paying tax. Why, under these proposals, will there still be some 60,000 profitable corporations which will not pay one cent of tax?
Is this fairness? Is this equity? Is this what the Minister of Finance meant when he said: "We all know that the tax system allows many profitable corporations to avoid paying a fair share of tax year after year"? The rhetoric is great but the reality, I am afraid, is something else. The fact is that some
60,000	very profitable corporations will still not pay a cent of tax. That means that $10 billion to $12 billion in profits do not create one cent of tax. Is that what the Government means when it talks about equity and fairness and restoring confidence in the tax system? It is no wonder that many Canadians feel ripped off by our tax system.
We hear Tory Members talking about the need to raise taxes because of the terrible deficit that the Liberals left behind. I sympathize with that. I think we have a problem with the deficit. It is much too large. The amount of interest we have to pay on the deficit every year is unacceptable, it is scandalous. However, I do not accept that we have this deficit because we have been spending and living beyond our means.
The OECD figures show that Canada spends less on social programs than any industrialized country in the world with the exception of the United States. We spend the second lowest percentage of our gross domestic product on social programs; old age pensions, housing, education, health, family allowance, and income support programs. We spend less as a percentage of our gross domestic product than Holland, Ireland, Italy, Germany, Sweden, Denmark, Japan, France, or Belgium.
Why is it that little Holland, with hardly any resources and an over-population, can spend more on its senior citizens, its education system, and its health system than can Canada, a young country with a population of young people and an abundance of resources? That is, I suggest, because the wealthy in this country have not been paying their fair share.
We have the deficit because there is $10 billion to $13 billion that does not generate one cent of tax. The deficit is not a result of overspending on senior citizens or the unemployed, or because we are spending too much on education or housing. I hear the Tories complain day after day that we are living beyond our means and must tighten our belts. There are food banks in every major city of this country. Yet the Tories still have the gall to tell us we are living beyond our means. I find that obscene. It is also obscene when the spokespersons from the large and wealthy corporations tell us that we must tighten our belts because we are living beyond our means and must reduce the deficit.
One year I received a letter from the President of the Royal Bank of Canada who advised us that we must tighten our belts because the deficit is out of control and government spending must be cut. Yet in 1982, 1 believe, the Royal Bank of Canada had over $365 million in profits and did not pay one cent in tax. In other words, a woman teller at the Royal Bank of Canada would have paid more in dollar and cents in tax than the Royal Bank of Canada. In fact, in that particular year the Royal Bank of Canada received a tax credit of some $20 million.
That is why we have a deficit. Yet we see a letter like that from the President of the Royal Bank of Canada saying that we must cut back on old age security and pensions, cut back on the benefits to the sick and elderly, cut back on social assistance and cut back on education while there are food banks and hungry people on the streets. That is obscene.
The Royal Bank of Canada is only one example. We asked the life insurance companies when they appeared before the committee when was the last time they paid tax. Most of them
July 19, 1988

could not remember because the last time they paid tax was in the mid 1970s. Billions of dollars in profits did not create one cent in tax. I suggest to the Tory Members that when they are concerned about the deficit, as they should be, they should examine why it exists. It is not because we are spending too much on social programs. It is shameful that we are second to last among all other industrialized countries in the world in terms of the amount we spend on social programs. When the elderly, the sick and the kids are blamed for the deficit, I say double shame.
The New Democratic Party Members on the Finance Committee co-operated with Government Members. I thought we produced a relatively good report. Unfortunately, the Government chose to ignore many of the recommendations of the committee. For example, it chose to ignore our recommendation of an advance corporate tax. It chose to ignore the recommendation of a minimum corporate tax to ensure that a company will indeed pay some tax if it makes a profit.
These companies enjoy a good business climate in this country. They depend upon educated young people to make profits for them and it is the public that has paid for their education. Is it not about time that the corporations paid something back to the public?
These corporations enjoy the road system and railway system in this country. Is it not time they paid for some of that? They enjoy many of the incentives governments have given them in grants and subsidies. Is it not time that they help pay for that?
We have seen the wealthy receive most of the tax breaks under the present Government. Despite all the rhetoric of the Minister of Finance about the unfairness of the existing tax system in which the rich were not paying their fair share and corporations making good profits were not contributing to the national purse, when it comes to the bottom line in Tory tax reform the Minister is taking the same action that he is denouncing. After tax reform, the rich in this country get even greater tax breaks than before.
Although the Government claims it will create more revenue from the corporate sector, already some of the Minister's estimates are out of whack. It is a farce for Government Members to talk about tax reform. It does not even measure up to the Minister's own standards.
It is true that compared to last year many Canadians will pay less tax. However, when we compare that to when the Tories came to power, most Canadians are paying more in tax. The corporations will be paying proportionately less in taxes than before.
When the Tories were elected, corporations made up some 20 per cent of tax revenues. In 1987-88, it was 15.6 per cent. After tax reform, it is projected that 17.2 per cent of all revenues will come from corporations. That is a far cry from the measly 20 per cent that existed before the Tories were elected.

Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague on his analysis of this Bill. We need to consider further the kind of progressive tax policy that is needed in this country. The Government has considered using tax credits rather than tax expenditures. Does a policy of tax credits rather than tax expenditures give a break to the poor?
There are more people living below the poverty line and paying tax now than ever before in the history of Canada. I do not believe it is acceptable to anyone that we ask the poor to pay our bills. We must give consideration to a tax reform system that redistributes income on an equitable basis. Has the Hon. Member considered the difference between tax credits and tax expenditures? Does it make this legislation any more progressive?

That is a very good question. In theory, yes, moving from a deduction to a credit is more progressive. It works in this way. Let us take a SI,000 deduction. If one is paying a tax rate of 50 per cent, a $1,000 deduction is worth $500. However, if one is a low-income earner and only paying, let us say, 25 per cent rate, that $1,000 deduction is only worth $250. The Government is taking away certain items as deductions and making them into credits so that the value of the credits are the same whether one is earning $100,000 and is in the 50 per cent bracket or one is earning $25,000 and is in the 25 per cent bracket. If the credit, let us say, is $200, it will be worth $200 if one is earning $100,000, and it is the same $200 if one is earning $25,000.
Having said that, it is interesting to see what the Minister of Finance and the Tory Government decided to move from a deduction to a credit and what they kept as a deduction. Those items that are important to lower and middle-income Canadians such as the personal exemption, the dependent's exemption and so on became credits. These are not too important to those earning $100,000 and more a year. What is important to them, of course, are the capital gains. What is important to them is the retirement savings plans, the RRSPs. These were not made into credits. These were still deductions.
It is interesting to note that 1 per cent of all taxpayers whose incomes are over $100,000 receive 34 per cent of all the capital gains. Capital gains do not become a credit. That still remains a deduction. Those with the higher incomes are the ones who will benefit. It is the same with retirement savings plans. These were not made into credits. They are still deductions. Those earning $100,000 per year will eventually be able to deduct $15,000 a year. If those people are in the 50 per cent bracket,

that means the Government will forgo some $7,500. Even if one is earning $30,000 and puts half of that into a RRSP, the way the Government has it rigged, they could not even claim that $15,000. But let us say for argument's sake that they could, and they are in the 30 per cent bracket. That $15,000 is only worth one-third or $5,000. It is worth $7,500 to the guy in the 50 per cent bracket but only $5,000 to the guy in the 30 per cent bracket. Again, in terms of capital gains and in terms of retirement plans, these did not become credits, they are still deductions, so while on the one hand we can say that moving personal exemptions into credits is progressive, where it really counted, the Government did not move.
The Government also took away some tax deductions that are important to middle-income earners. It just wiped them out. It did not even change them into credits. For example, the $500 deduction that was previously able to be deducted because of employment expenses is gone. The $1,000 interest deduction is eliminated. These are two deductions that are important to middle-income earners. They are not as important to those earning $100,000 or more per year. Deductions that are important to middle-income earners are gone and deductions that affect the poor have been turned into credits, but deductions that really benefit the rich still remain a deduction. I think that proves my thesis that this legislation is making the income tax system not more progressive but less progressive. It is making it regressive despite what the Minister of Finance initially claimed.

Canadian to save money and increase its purchasing power. We are setting up a new balance.

Well, it has not been forgotten by the majority of Canadians. That is why I remind government Members that, as Joe Howe fought for the principle of accountability, that principle of accountability will be brought to the forefront in the next election as it relates to their lack of action with regard to the subject of tax reform.

Members opposite know, and only know too well, that these rates are not enough. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the advantages of tax reform and to go on to more serious matters, after listening to the Hon. Member for the Liberal Party.
Mr. Speaker, I think I can safely state that most Members in this House are in favour of tax reform, in other words, a thorough revision of our tax system. Today's debate is about choosing the approach that is fair to the largest possible number of Canadian taxpayers.
The new legislation on tax reform is simply a reflection of the basic principles of lower tax rates and a broader and fairer tax base. The fairness of our system is the main concern of Canadian men and women. In fact, they will judge the new system in terms of this fundamental principle.
During the last ten years, Mr. Speaker, the system has failed to meet the legitimate expectations of Canadians with respect to fairness. So many people are wondering why their neighbour, who earns more than they do, is paying less in taxes. And why does the system contain so many loopholes that are of little benefit to the average Canadian unless he or she can afford to spend a lot of money on accountants and lawyers?
When the present Government came to power, we asked ourselves the same questions and, like so many Canadians, we were not satisfied with the answers. Consequently, we have eliminated a number of loopholes. The scam of the century was the scientific research tax credit program introduced by Marc Lalonde. We can say today, and we will say it again during the election campaign, that this was the scam of the century in Canada during the past twenty-five years.
Mr. Speaker, we introduced a minimum tax for Canadians on high incomes. We limited the option of redistributing income among members of the same family. We got rid of certain tax shelters involving investments in consumer goods such as yachts and pleasure vehicles. We put an end to the serious abuse of tax credits mentioned earlier, the scientific research tax credit of Mr. Lalonde.
However, in order to provide for a system whose fairness and effectiveness would be in line with the expectations of Canadian men and women, a complete revision of personal and corporate income tax and sales tax was necessary.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians told us that above all, they wanted their system to be fair and that they didn't want the majority of taxpayers to be deprived of certain advantages for the sake of a small group.
They told us that corporations and private citizens on high incomes should pay their fair share of income tax. They told us that people in the same income bracket should pay substantially the same amount of income tax. They said that above all,
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
Canadians on low incomes, especially the elderly, deserved fairer treatment.
Mr. Speaker, our tax reform reflects the desires of Canadian men and women. Perhaps I may point to one particular aspect of the reform which I feel illustrates the general principle of fairness which has been our constant guide. I am referring to benefits for the elderly.
Tax reform certainly meets the needs and aspirations of all Canadians, but it is especially beneficial for people 65 and over.
As of 1988, nine out of ten senior households will pay less income tax. In other words, about 1.3 million of the 1.4 million households that have at least one person aged 65 or over will pay less income tax. Furthermore, nearly 250,000 seniors will no longer pay income tax. That is what this Government has done and what is really important for our seniors.
The minimum income subject to income tax for seniors has also been changed. Depending on the type of income, the minimum for single people will be $11,430, or $645 more. For married couples, the minimum will rise by more than $2,000, to $19,010.
These changes are due to the reduction in tax rates and the conversion of personal exemptions and some deductions into tax credits.
This conversion is particularly beneficial for people aged 65 and over. Indeed, it is largely because of the greater value of credits that more than 90 per cent of senior households will pay less income tax.
Mr. Speaker, income tax credits will make the system fairer and more progressive. Members of this House know that exemptions are worth more to high-income individuals because they can reduce income that is subject to a higher marginal tax rate. On the other hand, credits directly reduce the amount of tax that seniors have to pay. They are worth the same for all taxpayers. For example, the new age credit for people 65 and over will be $550 in 1988. This represents a tax decrease of $550, whatever the level of income. It is a considerable additional tax saving for most seniors, because the exemption that the new credit replaces would only have been worth $450 for an individual declaring a taxable income under $25,500.
But for senior citizens with income of $55 000 or over, the former exemption would have been $775. Since some 80 per cent of senior taxpayers are at the bottom tax bracket, the new credit for the great majority of them means a significant improvement in terms of system fairness. Also, the basic personal exemption, that of the spouse and the disability credit all are worth more for most senior citizens than the exemptions they replace. Converting the pension income deduction into a 17 per cent credit up to a maximum $170 will still benefit those senior citizens whose taxable income is below $25 500. For most Canadians 65 and over, those credits will largely compensate for the elimination of the $1 000 deduction for investment income.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on tax reform. I have in front of me some criteria on how we should test tax reform. First, the burden of income and consumption taxes should be removed from low-income families and individuals. Canadians with incomes below the median or mid-way point for 1987, an estimated $13,000 for a single person and $42,000 for a family of four, should pay less total taxes, both income and consumption taxes. Only the taxpayer with an above average income should bear a heavier over-all tax burden under the new system. Tax reform must restore full indexation of tax brackets and credits, and the tax mix should not be altered to get more revenue from the regressive sales tax and less from income tax, which is the only progressive part of the over-all tax system. That is fairly clear. It is not too complicated a way of being able to judge legislation for tax reform.
We have looked over the years at what has happened to the tax system in Canada. There is no question in our minds that we certainly have ourselves into such a boondoggle that it is very difficult to get out of it. I think we need to look at some kind of criteria to see how we are to do it. Canadians must be terribly insulted by the kinds of reform the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has brought before this House. It is not reform. One thing we have done is to recognize the fact that additional revenues should not dependent on sales tax. As we look at the Bill before us, we find that more and more people with adequate incomes will have their taxes reduced. Sure, we have reduced the brackets from ten brackets to three brackets, but it is looking more and more like the flat income tax which the Fraser Institute, that right wing institute, wanted to implement over the years. The rich Conservatives certainly ascribe to that kind of philosophy and policy, but it is not the kind of policy average Canadians want to have implemented.
We must recognize that in 1984 when the Government came into office it said that it wanted to be fair and honest. It promised tax reform. If it had said since then that it had changed its mind and was not going to go ahead with it and that it would reduce taxes for the rich, then that would be okay. What is most upsetting is the sneaky way that this measure has been introduced. There has been a lot of rhetoric with respect to the introduction of this Bill.
If we look at what the Bill is all about, we see that what is being done is that a burden is being laid on the poor. A family earning $10,000 which was not paying any tax up until now will be paying about $1,100 to $1,200 in taxes in the form of sales tax in the next year.
What upsets me even more is that the return of taxes which was to be implemented January 1 will not come into operation until July 1. If the Government really thinks that Canadians are that gullible, then it has a great surprise coming to it. The electorate is not stupid. The electorate understands on what it is paying taxes and to whom it is paying them. Members of the public know that they will be getting a rebate even though they have been paying more taxes in the last four years than they have ever paid before. They will receive a rebate on July 1. That will be retroactive to January 1. That is an insult to their intelligence. It is a crass political operative type of program.
If we look at the loopholes about which the Government brags about closing, we know that some of them do not come into effect until 1991. What the Government is really saying is that perhaps after the next election we will be able to change the minds of some of the politicians and we will be able to continue with our tax breaks. That is not any way to run a railroad, and it is certainly not any way to run a country.
What Canadians have been looking at over the years in terms of tax reform is fairness and honesty. I travelled across the country when I was in another position which I held before I came here looking at the tax system. What I heard from Canadians right across the country was: "We do not mind paying taxes. But we really do object to knowing that people who are much better off than we are are paying less taxes than what we are paying". Canadians are not selfish or greedy. Perhaps the top 2 per cent of income earners might be. Perhaps their modus operandi is to ensure that they pay less tax and keep more for themselves. On the whole, as a society, we have clearly demonstrated over the years that we do not mind redistributing our income.
Another item which disturbs me is some of the rhetoric being used with regard to accountability and having to be careful in the corporate sector. The Auditor General for years has asked to have an accountability with regard to tax expenditures come forward to this House. In this way, for instance, if there was a tax expenditure in place we would know whether it was doing its job or not. The reason we have got into the science and film industry and other areas which have not necessarily worked is because there was no accountability and no measuring. To allow a tax exemption and not to look at its merits and not to see what it is doing to stimulate whatever industry it was put there for simply does not make sense.
We have heard that corporations are not paying taxes because three or four years ago they lost money and therefore they cannot afford to pay. If I had been unemployed for a couple of years and I consequently became employed, National Revenue would not say to me: "Because you did not have any
July 19, 1988

income for two or three years you do not have to pay any income tax this year". That is something which does not make any sense.
The rhetoric which has been used in the introduction of this Bill has been an attempt to make the system look very complex so that the ordinary person cannot understand it. The ordinary person can understand finances. They know how to run their country. They care about what happens to their public dollar. They will not be had by this type of faqade that says that we now have in front of us tax reform. We do not have that.
I have heard members of the Government say that they cannot tax corporations too high because if that is done there will be no incentive for reinvestment. It has been said that initiatives will be discouraged. Studies have shown that a measure of this type does not provide incentives to business. The level of taxation on corporations has no effect on whether or not they will reinvest.
In this respect we need only consider Japan, which has a very high level of productivity. The tax level in Japan is at 86 per cent. We realize that with this policy we do not have to be afraid to redistribute the income where there are massive profits being made. I will never understand the reluctance of people after they get into public office who say that, yes, it is an unfair system and, yes, we have to do something about it, and lo and behold they do nothing about it.
I know that there is a heavy dependency on the bureaucrats and the advisers when we have these types of Bills put before us. I think that our professionals should be well paid. I think politicians should be able to live within an adequate standard of living. I am not into a martyr syndrome at all. However, if we look at the people who deal with this type of policy, as well as every Member in this House-and I am not talking in a partisan way-we see that we are living a lot better than a lot of people living in our constituencies. The people who draw up these Bills very often have not been in that two room or three room accommodation where there are two or three children. They do not recognize that those people are still paying taxes.
I cannot express to Hon. Members how much it upsets me when I realize that very low-income people are paying taxes. By flattening out the tax system and by going to a consumption tax what we are really doing is saying: "Okay, poor, you have paid some now but we are really going to get you every time you buy something-and you can't wait for a sale because you do not have any extra cash. We'll get you then. You'll have to pay at that point in time". That is not a compassionate type of policy. This is not a compassionate type of Bill.
More important, this is not an intelligent piece of legislation when we consider it in terms of reinvestment in our country and in terms of stimulating the economy through the tax system. What we have in front of us is a Bill that does not provide us with the type of accountability for which we are looking. It is a Bill which states that we do not have to measure what the incentives were.
Income Tax Act and Related Acts
A great many of my constituents in Hamilton Mountain are over the age of 65.1 have heard various Members of the House address the income of senior citizens. Wiping out the $1,000 investment exemption does not mean a thing to people who have large incomes and large investments. For the ordinary working person who has invested, for example, seniors who are receiving $1,000 annually, they have looked at it as part of their income. As one gentleman said to me, it has been the way in which he has been able to provide Christmas for his family. He knows that with this money he can get things for his grandchildren and feel comfortable about it. Now that $1,000 is gone. It is being taxed. When bureaucrats look at those types of things and decide that they have to get rid of some exemptions, they take a whole page and get rid of them. Not a lot of thought went into the recommendation to take away that $1,000. It is not the upper-income earner who is hurt, it is the ordinary person who is hurt by that type of policy.
There has been much talk about the number of people who will drop from the tax lists. We must look at the number of people who came onto the tax roll since 1984. All of a sudden they are to be dropped and we say that that is good. That does not make any sense. That is not reform, but regression to where we were. I hear the Conservatives saying that they want to be different from the Liberals, and they are going back to where the Liberals were. That is not what we want.
Certainly, if we are going to look at tax reform, we must look at starting to pay taxes at the upper end of our society so that income tax is used as a real tool for redistribution of income. We should not play games with each other. We have a very rich country with many resources. Yet 40 per cent of the clients of the soup kitchens in our major cities are children. Here we have a tax Bill in front of us that is putting a burden on families with children, and is kinder to a two-income couple who are childless. That is not the type of tax reform that Canadians are looking for.
To redistribute the income we must look at who taxes are hitting most. When we burden the poor we are making society non-functioning, and putting a bigger burden on people generally. The cry for more housing is heard. Surely no one present does not recognize the fact that soup kitchens are a cancer in our society and in our cities. People are lining up at soup kitchens and are beholden to each one of us for the crumbs from our table, and we are sitting here with a tax Bill where our own tax rate will be reduced. Most of us are at the upper end of the scale and we will pay less. Sure, it is great for us, but what is happening to the population is really hurting. They are not getting any breaks from this Bill. All they will receive are more burdens.
Further, there is an attempt by the Government to put a veil around all of this. It states that it will go to the second step after the election; the second step after we know we have you

Income Tax Act and Related Acts
and we will really lay it on you. I have news for the Government. Canadians are not that gullible and they certainly will not swallow that.
We must seriously look at some of the companies that are not paying any tax at all. I have here a list for 1986 of income figures for certain companies. In 1986 Alcan Aluminum on income totalling $220 million received a tax credit of $32 million; Brascan on income totalling $187 million received a tax credit of $2.3 million; Power Financial on income of $132 million received a tax credit of $1 million; Xerox Canada on income totalling $115 million received a tax credit of $10.8 million. I am sure we all contribute to that company's income in our offices. Bramalea on an income totalling $51 million, no taxes were paid; Wardair on an income totalling $70 million, no taxes were paid. In 1987 Carena-Bancorp on income totalling $37 million, no taxes were paid. Hudson's Bay Company, a company we all contribute to as consumers, had income totalling $50 million, and a tax credit of $15.7 million; Seco-Camp on income totalling $43 million, no taxes were paid; Union Carbide Canada on income totalling $28 million, no taxes were paid.
These are not the types of policies that we think are tax reform. We certainly do think that there are resources in this country, and that we can redistribute that economy in a more fair way in order that every Canadian citizen has the ability to have a quality of life with some dignity.
I am certainly not giving any credit to the Liberals because they got us into this mess. They started with the tax expenditures and there was no accountability. When the Carter Commission was conducted in 1967 it was appointed by a Tory Government. When it came to reporting predominantly business commission and it was decided that there must be accountability in the tax system, Bay Street got into the act. The lobbying took place and they all backed away. Who was hurt? The ordinary Canadian. We knew in 1967 that we were in a mess and we dug ourselves deeper and deeper into it. We are giving more corporate give-aways and consistently putting a greater burden on the poor. That is not tax reform. The people of Canada will not be fooled by it.

In the case of a single individual aged 65 and over prior to tax reform he or she started paying tax at $10,785; after tax reform it will be $11,430. There is a substantial difference, and the Hon. Member is quite well aware of that. I am sure that she does not want to leave a false impression.
There are some other facts as well that I know that she is aware of and that she would not want to leave a false impression about. One has to do with what is happening again with the tax cuts for couples, both earning income, with two children 18 and under. In fact, the tax refunds go up for people earning a family income of $10,000, by $280 for a $15,000-a-year couple. They go up for a $20,000-a-year couple by 59 per cent. That is a percentage of tax of 59 per cent.
In the case of a family earning $25,000, it goes up by 21.6 per cent. I am drawing to a close, but as your income goes up the percentage of savings goes down. At $30,000, it is only 11.4 per cent. At $75,000 it is only 5.9 per cent. I know that the Hon. Member does not want to leave a false impression. I know that she wants to stand up now to correct that false impression and to make it quite clear that not only are Canadians going to benefit under this tax reform package, but they will have already benefited under the economic policies of the Government as there has been a reduction in the number of Canadians living below the poverty level since it took office of 525,000 people.
In addition, the average family income has climbed, in spite of tax changes, by $1,600 in real terms since this Government took office. I know that the Hon. Member wants to correct the record and to applaud the Government for its fine work.

Certainly, if you look at the falling threshold you recognize that tax reform will provide only a temporary respite from the downward trend in the tax-paying threshold for the simple reason that deindexation has taken place. It also depends on where you are comparing it from, whether from 1984 or from 1988. After all the regressive policies have been put in, from 1984 to 1988 you will see that it makes a big difference. However, if you just take 1988, you will see that it lifts the tax threshold up to $5,971, or 54 per cent of the poverty line. But partial indexation of the tax system pushes it back down after 1988. By 1991, federal income tax applies to earnings of $5,448, or just under half the poverty line.
